💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, whole wheat bread used to be the gold standard of quick, healthy carbs.
  • It has been revealed that as a dietitian, I see this showdown between whole wheat and sourdough all the time.
  • Whole wheat is exactly what it sounds like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, whole wheat bread used to be the gold standard of quick, healthy carbs. Unlike white bread, it uses flour milled from the entire wheat kernel, providing extra fiber and vitamins. But sourdough has exploded in popularity over the past decade, offering a seemingly more natural option made from just sourdough starter, flour, and water. Is this ancient breadmaking method healthier than whole wheat, even if it uses white flour?

It has been revealed that as a dietitian, I see this showdown between whole wheat and sourdough all the time. People wonder if the rustic, tangy charm of sourdough beats the wholesome, fiber-packed power of whole wheat. Let’s slice into the details and figure out which loaf deserves a spot on your counter.

Whole wheat is exactly what it sounds like. This bread is made using flour from the entire wheat kernel—the bran, germ, and endosperm. Here’s what that means:.

Because it includes all parts of the kernel, 100% whole wheat bread delivers fiber, essential vitamins like folate and niacin, and notable minerals such as iron and magnesium. That fiber helps you feel satisfied after eating, supports digestion, and can support blood sugar management and heart health. This combination makes this particular bread a smart, nutrient-dense choice for everyday eating.

Industry observers note that it’s a reliable, widely available, research-backed whole grain—and most Americans don’t eat the recommended servings of whole grains every day, which the USDA suggests is more than half of the grains we eat. So, choosing whole-grain bread can help people meet this recommendation.

Sources indicate that it seems like everyone and their mother got into baking sourdough a few years ago. We all know it’s delicious, but what makes it special from a health perspective isn't just its ingredients—it’s how it is made.

Industry observers note that sourdough isn’t defined by a specific type of flour. You can make it with all-purpose, rye, or whole-wheat flour; some loaves use enriched/fortified flour for an extra boost of iron and B vitamins. And its magic lies in the fermentation process. Instead of commercial yeast, sourdough relies on a “starter,” which is a living mix of wild yeast and beneficial bacteria (specifically, lactobacilli).

This fermentation process does some pretty amazing things:.

In a side-by-side battle, let's see which bread comes out on top:.

You don’t have to pick a single winner.

If your primary goal is to maximize your fiber intake and get a consistent, nutrient-packed loaf, 100% whole wheat is an excellent choice.

If you're looking for a bread that’s easier to digest and offers enhanced mineral absorption, deliciously tangy sourdough is your go-to.

But it is possible to have the best of both worlds. Grab (or bake) a sourdough bread made with 100% whole wheat flour for fiber, nutrient density, and fermentation perks.

Whether you’re Team Sourdough or Team Whole Wheat, there’s one universal truth: your body, and let’s be honest, your soul, will thank you. Because we all know that carbs are good for the soul.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Safe Word is a series highlighting the latest trends in the jewelry market, keeping you up to date on all things that sparkle and shine.

November’s jewelry releases are looking both backward and forward, with designers revisiting their roots, reworking archival ideas, and stepping into entirely newly introduced territory. First up, Quentin Jones is taking her surrealist art off the wall and onto the body with ‘Nocturne’, her first jewelry collection; Pomellato reaches back to 1997 to revive “Moneta Orientale” as a colorful modern talisman; David Yurman celebrates the magic of a New York holiday with Michael B. Jordan, Yerin Ha, and Inde Navarrette; Vhernier revisits its iconic “Trottola” design with new proportions and contrasting materials; Di Volpe reinterprets the classic tennis bracelet with customizable gemstones in “DiSegno”; Brent Neale transforms the classic bow into sculptural fine jewelry with “Wrap It Up”; and Kendra Scott launches the new “Kendra Scott Collection,” reimagining her signature Spike motif as a personal talisman. From archival revivals and meaningful motifs to innovative designs and new creative directions, November’s launches prove that sometimes the best way forward starts with looking back. For the rest of the month, we’ve got you covered on all the jewelry-related happenings worth knowing about.

Quentin Jones Turns Her Art Into Jewelry.

Quentin Jones is taking her art off the wall and onto the body with “Nocturne,” the first jewelry collection from House of Quentin Jones. Following the multidisciplinary artist’s debut of surrealist ceramics and tapestries last year, the new collection transforms recurring gestures and symbols from her work into sculptural collars, cuffs, armbands, pendants, chains, and earrings. Eyes, hands, stars, moons, tears, and knots take shape in silver and gold vermeil alongside freshwater pearls, onyx, opals, jade, glass, and silk tassels, giving the pieces a dreamlike, talismanic quality. Beginning as drawings and hand collages in Jones’s Brooklyn studio, each design carries her surrealist visual language into wearable form, further blurring the line between art, design, and fashion.

Kendra Scott Rolls out an Eponymous Collection.

Kendra Scott is offering a more personal look into her design world with the launch of the “Kendra Scott Collection,” a upcoming line spanning fashion and fine jewelry. Its first edition, “The Spike,” revisits a silhouette the designer has worn throughout her career as a personal symbol of strength, confidence, and conviction. Inspired by nature and the radiance of the night sky, the collection translates the pointed motif into sculptural necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and charms, balancing bold proportions with intricate craftsmanship. Fashion jewelry incorporates tiger’s eye, malachite, and turquoise, while fine jewelry introduces lab-grown diamonds, pavé detailing, labradorite, and lapis. From statement-making links to delicate diamond charms, the collection offers a new interpretation of Scott’s longtime signature, inviting wearers to make the symbol their own.

Alison Lou’s ‘Newly introduced Wave’ Collection Experiments With New Materials.

Alison Lou is entering a new chapter with “New Wave,” a fine jewelry collection that introduces unexpected materials and a fresh approach to the designer’s signature playful aesthetic. Exploring the relationship between movement and form, the collection pairs lightweight titanium and ceramic with lab-grown diamonds, creating fluid, sculptural silhouettes that curve and catch the light. Available in Fig and Denim Blue colorways, the designs include wavy rings, diamond-accented signets, delicate thread necklaces, and statement drop earrings. With its unconventional materials and easy-to-wear designs, “New Wave” brings a new sense of movement to Alison Lou’s everyday jewelry.

Jenny Bird and Emese Gormley Partner on the Anyu Ring.

Jenny Bird is expanding her JB FINE collection with a new collaboration featuring lifestyle creator and Lipstick on the Rim podcast host Emese Gormley. Named in honor of Gormley’s mother, the Anyu Ring offers a personal take on the classic signet, featuring three lab-grown baguette diamonds set in 14-karat yellow or white gold. The understated design combines the timeless appeal of a signet ring with a sentimental tribute to family, bringing a new perspective to Bird’s growing fine jewelry offering. Available exclusively on Jenny Bird’s website, the collaboration makes a case for jewelry that feels as meaningful as it looks.

Pomellato Revives Its 1997 Moneta Orientale Pendant as a Colorful Talisman.

According to recent reports, pomellato is looking to its archives for its latest good-luck charm. For the newest chapter of “Memorie d’Archivio,” the maison revives Moneta Orientale, a 1997 pendant inspired by the ancient symbolism of a circle surrounding a square, representing the harmony between heaven and earth. Made in 33 stone-and-pavé combinations, the design pairs colorful hard stones including black jade, amazonite, sodalite, rhodochrosite, and labradorite with Pomellato’s signature irregular pavé of diamonds, sapphires, rubies, and more. Offered in two proportions, each pendant transforms the archival motif into a modern talisman for prosperity and protection.

Bibi van der Velden Makes Her High Jewelry Debut With ‘Eclipse’.

Bibi van der Velden is entering a new era with “Eclipse,” the designer’s first high jewelry collection and most refined exploration of diamonds to date. Inspired by the fleeting moment when light gives way to darkness, the collection includes two six-piece suites: one in white diamonds and another defined by an ombré of diamonds into gray spinels deepening into black. Van der Velden’s signature alligator motif is abstracted into fluid, sculptural silhouettes, with scales engraved into the white gold on the reverse of each piece. “With Eclipse, I wanted to take those familiar elements and transform them into something more abstract and sculptural,” she notes. “It’s a collection about transformation, which has always been at the heart of my work.”.

Aflalo and Leandra Medine Cohen Turn Everyday Indulgences Into Fine Jewelry.

Aflalo is finding the humor in our obsession with wellness with “The Vanities,” a new two-piece fine jewelry capsule designed exclusively by Leandra Medine Cohen. Playing with the contradiction between longevity and life’s little indulgences, the collection transforms two unlikely everyday accessories into precious objects. The Memento Mori is a 14-karat yellow gold cigar band set with more than four carats of diamonds, designed to slip over an Oura Ring, while The Libertine is a sterling silver pendant case adorned with diamonds and a wild-haired woman outlined in gold, designed to hold nicotine pouches or other small essentials. Equal parts extravagant and irreverent, the collection makes a playful case for enjoying life’s pleasures without sacrificing personal style.

Julia Berolzheimer’s Hart Jewelry Collection Draws on Childhood Memories.

Hart is teaming up with Julia Berolzheimer for a latest jewelry collection that celebrates the art of the stack. Inspired by Berolzheimer’s childhood memories of her grandmother’s California ranch and her collection of Art Deco minaudières, the collaboration brings together whimsical charms, colorful gemstones, and meaningful talismans designed to be mixed, layered, and restyled. Botanical motifs take shape in Tree of Life coins, daisies, bees, and fruit-inspired charms, while carnelian, turquoise, and pink opal add playful pops of color. One standout is the Perfume Vesta Case, a modern interpretation of a Victorian-era accessory that can hold a sample-sized fragrance and hang alongside other charms. With interchangeable chains, cords, and pendants, the collection makes a case for jewelry that feels just as personal as the memories behind it.

David Yurman Captures the Magic of a Fresh York Holiday.

David Yurman is celebrating the magic of the holidays in Newly introduced York City with a new campaign featuring global brand ambassador Michael B. Jordan alongside actresses Yerin Ha and Inde Navarrette. Set against a snow-covered Washington Square Park, the campaign captures a series of quintessential New York moments, from Jordan and Ha facing off in a spirited card game to Navarrette hailing a cab in search of the perfect holiday gift. Throughout the campaign, the cast wears some of the house’s most recognizable designs, including 18-karat gold Cable bracelets and pieces from the “Starburst” and “Armory” collections. Directed by Bradford Young and photographed by Drew Vickers, the campaign brings together the spirit of the city, the joy of togetherness, and the timeless appeal of David Yurman’s jewelry.

Vhernier Reintroduces Its Iconic ‘Trottola’ Design With Fresh Proportions.

Vhernier is revisiting one of its most recognizable designs with a latest interpretation of “Trottola,” the sculptural collection originally introduced in 2003. Inspired by the continuous motion of a spinning top, the latest designs play with proportions, contrasting materials, and asymmetrical shapes across rings, bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Polished rose gold meets glossy black jet, with select pieces featuring diamond pavé for an added contrast of light and dark. The collection also focuses on versatility, from rings designed for stacking to convertible earclips that can be worn as studs or dangling earrings. With its fluid forms and unexpected material combinations, “Trottola” brings a fresh perspective to Vhernier’s signature sculptural approach to jewelry.

Di Volpe Reinvents the Tennis Bracelet.

Di Volpe is rethinking the classic tennis bracelet with “DiSegno,” a upcoming customizable fine jewelry system designed to change with its wearer. Using concealed, patent-pending connections, individual cultured diamonds and gemstones, called Elements, can be removed, rearranged, or added by hand, allowing wearers to transform bracelets into necklaces or earrings without compromising the seamless look of traditional tennis jewelry. The collection debuts with 28 stone-and-cut combinations, including rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and diamonds, alongside a limited-edition collaboration with Lebanese artist Ali Cha’aban featuring five sculptural designs. With new cuts, colors, and artist collaborations planned for future releases, “DiSegno” makes the case for fine jewelry that’s never quite finished.

Brent Neale Riffs on the Bow in Fine Jewelry.

Brent Neale is putting a bow on the holiday season with “Wrap It Up,” a latest fine jewelry collection that transforms the familiar ribbon motif into sculptural works of art. Drawing inspiration from Old Hollywood glamour and the femininity of the 1960s, the designer plays with the contrast between rigid precious metals and the soft movement of fabric, crafting bows that twist, curl, and unfurl in 18-karat gold and platinum. Colored gemstones sit nestled within the ribbon-like forms, while pavé diamonds accentuate every curve and fold. Equal parts playful and precious, the collection brings a little gift-wrapped glamour to the jewelry box.

Grace Winfrey’s ‘Poppy Fortuna’ Collection Reimagines Good-Luck Charms.

Industry observers note that grace Winfrey is bringing a little extra luck to the jewelry box with “Poppy Fortuna,” a upcoming fine jewelry collection inspired by the natural beauty of the Italian landscape and symbols of good fortune. Scarlet poppies, sunflowers, bees, four-leaf clovers, horseshoes, and ladybugs come to life through vibrant gemstones and intricate pavé, creating miniature mosaics of color and texture. Highlights include a Lucky Bangle combining three good-luck charms, sculptural sunflower earrings with tiny ladybugs tucked into their petals, and layered charm necklaces designed to feel like modern keepsakes. Handcrafted in New York City, each piece transforms familiar symbols of prosperity, protection, and happiness into playful, colorful works of art.

Robinson Pelham Channels ’90s Glamour for Its Anniversary.

According to recent reports, robinson Pelham is closing out its 30th anniversary celebrations with “Suite 96,” a new campaign and collection launch inspired by the glamour of late-’90s London. Set inside a private suite at St. James’s Hotel & Club in Mayfair, the campaign considers jewelry the ultimate room service, with diamonds arriving on trays, gold spilling out of wardrobes, and plenty of pieces to layer before a night out. At the center is “Studio 30,” a four-piece anniversary collection featuring diamond necklaces and statement earrings, including the sculptural Via and Hira necklaces, cascading diamond drops, and the bold Solstice Supreme. Alongside the anniversary designs, the house introduces new collections and additions to existing favorites, from chunky gold links and graphic heart rings to colorful enamel and gemstone combinations. Together, the debuts celebrate three decades of Robinson Pelham’s bold, playful approach to fine jewelry.

Le Vian and Jared Revive Georgian-Era Romance.

It has been revealed that le Vian is bringing a little old-world romance to Jared Jewelers with its upcoming exclusive “Georgian Chocolate & Nude Diamonds” collection. Inspired by the candlelit jewels of the Georgian era, when jewelry was designed to capture and reflect the warmth of natural light, the collection rethinks historic buttercup settings in polished Honey Gold, with eight rounded prongs framing each natural diamond. The designs pair Le Vian’s signature Chocolate and Nude Diamonds with warm gold detailing across solitaire rings, anniversary bands, tennis bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Select styles introduce colorful gemstones including Chocolate Quartz, Green Apple Peridot, and Grape Amethyst, giving the vintage-inspired silhouettes a contemporary upgrade. With its sculptural settings and warm-toned stones, the collection brings the romance of antique jewelry into the present.

Wempe’s ‘Au:thentic’ Celebrates the Art of Goldsmithing.

Wempe’s latest gender-inclusive fine jewelry collection, “Au:thentic,” puts craftsmanship front and center, finding inspiration in the foundational skills taught to aspiring goldsmiths. The collection takes its shape from the jump ring, one of the first techniques Patrick Sieroslawski learned as an apprentice more than 22 years ago, translating its form to necklaces, bracelets, rings, earrings, and pendants. Handcrafted at Wempe’s atelier in Germany, the pieces come in 18-karat yellow, white, and rose gold, with select styles set with diamonds. “Au:thentic” also marks the beginning of a multiyear rollout, with three additional chapters set to expand on its design language through twists, wraps, and interlocking links.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a kid who grew up making weekly trips to Boston Market, I’m no stranger to getting mashed potatoes to go. While the chain is a lot harder to find these days, I can still turn to a handful of others when I don’t feel like peeling potatoes and making a batch myself. I might not be rushing to supply my Thanksgiving dinner table with takeout mashed potatoes, but I’m certainly not averse to ordering some to dip my fried chicken into.

According to recent reports, I ordered taters from three local fast-food chains to see which one passes muster for texture, seasoning, and all-around flavor. Here’s how it all went down.

According to recent reports, along with Boston Market, I grew up as a regular at KFC. Sadly, its mashed potatoes didn't hit quite as well as I remember. Here, you can order mashed potatoes with or without gravy (the only chain on this list with a gravy-free option), but for this tasting, I opted for the topped version. While they were super creamy, I'd argue they're almost too creamy. They could benefit from a bit more texture and structure. I also found them a bit bland.

I appreciated the gravy, which kept the potatoes from tasting dry, but the potatoes themselves weren't much to write home about.

Popeyes’ mashed potatoes come topped with Cajun gravy, setting them apart from your standard dish. I really enjoyed the flavor of the gravy—it was almost reminiscent of gumbo—and I thought it added a unique element to the mashed potatoes. There was a tiny hint of spice here that also worked really well.

The potatoes are very creamy but thicker than KFC's, and overall, they were more satisfying in terms of both texture and flavor.

According to recent reports, jollibee's taters were quite good and, hands down, the most classic iteration of the bunch. I liked that you could see actual pieces of potato skin in the mashed potatoes. The gravy also tasted the most traditional, with an almost turkey-like flavor. Notably, these were the least creamy potatoes of the three I tried, but thanks to the gravy, they didn't taste dry.

However, the scoop of actual mashed potatoes was pretty meager, and they were drowned in the gravy. Still, I would choose these over the others when I'm looking for that quintessential gravy-and-mashed combo.

And for the occasion, Florence Pugh embraced the story’s time period with a sculptural, Victorian look with over-the-top power shoulders.

Designed by Harris Reed, the ensemble echoed classic Victorian mourning dressing, a custom popularized by Queen Victoria after the 1861 death of her husband, Prince Albert. (Just one year before the first chapter of East of Eden takes place.) The modest style required all-black fabrics, high necklines, and long sleeves—all of which can be seen in Pugh’s tailored peplum jacket, with its V-notch stand collar and fabric-covered buttons. Makeup artist Alex Babsky finished things off with a moody deep-red lipstick, a custom shade he mixed together himself.

According to recent reports, pugh was joined by co-star Christopher Abbott and series creator Zoe Kazan, who adapted John Steinbeck’s 1952 novel for the screen. The Little Women actor not only starred in the 2026 interpretation, but also served as executive producer. She brought a nuanced performance to the role of Cathy, who has traditionally been seen as a soulless antagonist, but here was given a more complex, compelling backstory that humanized her.

Whether hitting the red carpet in a little lingerie-inspired slip or dressing up a long ivory robe for an event, Dakota Johnson has long loved a good pajama dressing moment. And on Thursday night, she gave her go-to style another spin—this time with a breezy two-piece set that could seriously take her from a night out to a night in.

Courtesy of Italian label Loretta Caponi, the ensemble was composed of a long-sleeve midi dress and relaxed trousers, each crafted from black satin, adorned with delicate gold floral embroidery, and trimmed with scalloped lace. The loose dress, with its choker collar, deep V neckline and drop shoulders, was secured in the front by a line of buttons—which Johnson left undone, wearing the piece as a robe. Underneath, the Fifty Shades of Grey actor embraced another one of her favorite trends—naked dressing—with a sheer black lace cami that was embroidered with a floral design of its own. And, for a third pop of pattern, she grabbed a small leopard-print Valentino bag.

Johnson wore the look to Thursday night’s Los Angeles screening of Flesh Impact, Maggie Gyllenhaal’s forthcoming short film that imagines what Marilyn Monroe’s life might have been like had she lived to be 100 years old. For the project, Johnson transformed into Monroe at the height of her fame, blonde hair and all. It premiered at Venice Film Festival in September, though a theatrical or streaming release date has not yet been revealed.

Packing for these trips, however, can be a puzzle. You'll want lots of base layers to keep warm, outerwear that's both functional and stylish, cozy loungewear for game nights and hanging by the fire, and festive looks for photo-op-worthy nights out. Oh, and you need it to all fit in your suitcase or weekend bag.

Recent findings suggest that no worries! Right now, Target is stocked with versatile pieces that can help you check all those boxes and make planning—and packing—your fits easy. Think affordable, 100 percent cashmere sweaters, faux fur coats, and cold-weather accessories in this season's hottest hues. Here, we outline a holiday travel packing list filled with our top cozy, stylish finds from Target.

Cashmere is warm, but not bulky, and a natural, breathable fiber that doesn't require frequent washing, making it ideal for your winter travel wardrobe. A crewneck cardigan in a poppy red can look festive at holiday gatherings or serve as a personality piece when paired with royal purple or prints. A striped blue crewneck pullover feels casual yet cool with jeans or trousers, while a simple black option can be dressed up for a dinner out.

A New Day Women's Cashmere Crewneck Pullover Sweater Black.

A Fresh Day Women's Cashmere Crewneck Pullover Sweater Blue Striped.

Rather than treating your jacket like an afterthought, invest in a statement piece: A faux suede and shearling coat in a deep, espresso brown can feel like a vintage '60s find, while an ivory faux fur option will command attention while keeping you warm. A puffer with a fun and festive print can be a fashion-forward choice for ski trips.

Universal Thread Women's Shearling Fashion Coat.

Universal Thread Women's Faux Fur Coat.

Wild Fable Women's Puffer Jacket.

When faced with frigid temps, you'll want to make sure you pack the works: scarves, hats, and gloves. These accessories don't need to be purely utilitarian—they can add a pop of personality to your outfit while keeping you cozy. A knit cashmere triangle scarf in an on-trend powder blue will pop against a brown coat or sweater, while a purple cashmere beanie adds a playful touch to all-black outerwear. If you prefer vintage looks, an aviator-style hat with a faux shearling brim is an unexpected choice, while black leather mittens with a faux fur cuff have just the right amount of edge.

A Newly introduced Day Faux Fur Cuff Mittens Black.

For dinners out, a simple top like a black satin halter can elevate a pair of jeans and will take up minimal space in your bag. If your style is more edgy, skip the frill in favor of a corset top, mini skirt, and tall boots.

Wild Fable High Neck Lace Velvet Mini Dress.

Flare leggings and a striped fleece are comfortable enough to wear while relaxing on the couch, but will look put together if you bump into someone from high school when you're out running last-minute holiday errands. If you prefer snuggling up in sweats, pack at least one hoodie with personality in the form of a graphic print. Layer a cute cami with lace trim underneath for a cozy yet styled look.

Look for clothes that add warmth without adding bulk, such as a cashmere crewneck sweater. If you're flying this holiday season, wear your thickest items, like your coat and boots, on the plane.

Industry observers note that bold outerwear is on trend for 2026. Look for coats that make a statement with materials such as faux fur and silhouettes including cinched waists.

A simple black sweater can be a blank canvas for your trip. Wear it with jeans and comfortable shoes while you sightsee, then add wide-leg trousers and gold jewelry for a dinner out. And up until this morning, Amazon MGM and director Denis Villeneuve have not confirmed one. single. thing. But it’s official: Robert Pattinson is the fresh James Bond.

Sources indicate that the rumor mill has been churning for months. Several actors screen-tested for the iconic role, including Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, but Robert Pattinson was an eleventh hour surprise. Matthew Belloni wrote in Puck News last week that there was reason to think Robert is favored to become the next 007.

More sources explained that since Robert’s “test deal was so difficult to close,” people close to the situation were “wondering why the filmmakers would bother if they didn’t really want him.”.

It has been revealed that there’s been so much discourse about whether or not Bond should be an established household name (traditionally, he isn’t), with former casting director Debbie McWilliams—who cast the last three Bonds—telling The Independent, “It is absolutely essential that he retains a total enigma. I don’t want to see any of them as Bond because we now know so much about them. We want to know as little about them personally as possible, because that what spies are. We don’t need to know where he goes shopping or who his parents are, or where he lives. We never want to see him at home. And a vital element of the whole thing is his job description. He’s licensed to kill, and we have to believe that he can do that. If you don’t, then you’ve lost the audience.”.

Casting Robert Pattinson definitely challenges that approach, but we’ll see how it goes!

Upside-down tartlets went viral on social media, but they’re the party app we’re forever obsessed with. The mushrooms:You can find mushrooms used in two different ways here: both sliced and in a creamy, cheesy filling. The filling starts with a classic combination of minced mushrooms and shallots known as a duxelles (the very same mixture you can find at the base of a beef Wellington). To make this filling more mushroom soup-esque, we supplement it with Gùyere, heavy cream, and either sour cream or crème fraîche. The tangy dairy offsets some of the richness of the pastry while still containing enough fat to avoid curdling in the oven.

The pastry:When working with puff pastry, it’s notable that you avoid prolonged exposure to heat. The dough is stacked with layers and layers of cold butter, which should melt and produce steam in the oven to create that signature flaky texture. Allowing that butter to melt while the dough sits on the counter will sacrifice that essential puff. If you notice your pastry start to warm up or stick to the counter, transfer it to a parchment-lined baking sheet, and let it cool down in the refrigerator for 10 to 15 minutes before you start working with it again.

It has been revealed that make ahead:The best part about this recipe is that you can make most of the components ahead of time. The mushroom filling can be made up to 3 days in advance, while the puff pastry squares can be cut and refrigerated up to a day before serving.

Dressing Like Your Boyfriend Is Actually Fine

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that is it so wrong to dress like your boyfriend?
  • I personally think it’s a silly argument given that Bella Hadid is one of the most notable supermodels with an eccentric, well-documented high-fashion sense of style.
  • The same argument has been made about Ariana Grande, Kim Kardashian, and, more recently (even by her own sisters, who do the same thing), Kourtney Kardashian.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that is it so wrong to dress like your boyfriend? Clearly, the internet thinks so. Most recently, Bella Hadid has found herself at the center of this conversation, with people highlighting her various boyfriend eras like some sort of sartorial identity crisis. From the emo-adjacent vibes when she dated the singer, The Weeknd, to the cowboy-rodeo-chic aesthetic with Adan Banuelos, and now her hockey-game-attending, matching outfit moment with newly introduced man Nathan Lacy, Bella has seemingly been accused of basing her clothes after her romantic partners.

I personally think it’s a silly argument given that Bella Hadid is one of the most notable supermodels with an eccentric, well-documented high-fashion sense of style. She was awarded Lyst’s 2022 Most Powerful Dresser, and she famously styles much of her own day-to-day looks. So who cares if, during a particular season of her life, she wants to tap into the aesthetic of the man she’s dating?

The same argument has been made about Ariana Grande, Kim Kardashian, and, more recently (even by her own sisters, who do the same thing), Kourtney Kardashian. Ariana’s personal style has never particularly screamed fashion girl to me, and I’m a huge proponent of the idea that not everyone needs to be one anyway. Grande works with stylists to build her looks, so if on her off days she wants to dress in tandem with her beau, there’s truly nothing wrong with that.

Kim Kardashian, meanwhile, notoriously skyrocketed into the high-fashion space during her relationship with Kanye West. To this day, Kim gives style credits to Kanye’s eye for fashion and his introducing her to the world she so desperately wanted to be part of. Did she take what he taught her and expand upon it, eventually establishing herself as a fashion mogul in her own right? Yes. So technically in the long term, borrowing an aesthetic from her boyfriend then husband clearly worked out for her.

And while I personally wouldn’t wear Kourtney’s ultra-rock-girlfriend aesthetic, I actually think it's fun. After spending a decade being terrorized by Scott Disick (terrible boyfriend, excellent family friend to her sisters), I think it’s perfectly fine for my girl to enjoy someone so much she clearly feels safe enough to wrap herself in his sartorial aesthetic.

Sources indicate that this idea that women are in the wrong for “adopting” their man’s fashion seems uninteresting to me. If anything, women should be stealing men’s aesthetics and making them their own more often. There's something cheeky about the whole thing, a small flip of patriarchy on its head. How often do we see the internet go viral over the invisible labor women put into the men they date? Making their style better, recommending the haircut that best frames their face, teaching them how to groom themselves. It’s always give, give, give. So why not take something too? Because the next video down my timeline after those labor of love, “girlfriend effect” ones is women complaining about men taking everything they gave in a relationship (from hair and clothing reccs) and bringing it to the next woman.

There's something rather liberating about having your own style to return to while allowing yourself to experiment with whatever your boyfriend of the moment is into. It’s like playing dress-up. You’re enjoying a man, his world, and even his wardrobe, without having to make any of it your permanent identity—simply trying it out like free samples of ice cream. And when he’s no longer serving you, you move on. Thank you, next, as Miss Grande indicates.

Because women are so often expected to do the emotional and personal-care work in relationships, it’s honestly fine to me seeing these celebrities lean into their boyfriends’ fashion sense. (Side note: Incredible that these men have a style at all—it can be sartorially bleak out there!) Maybe his hockey jerseys look good on you. Maybe his leather jackets are better than yours. Maybe you just like the way you look in a cowboy hat right now.

It isn’t hurting anyone. And if anything, the most radical part of all is letting the men, for once, shape the fashion in their relationship. High time we all start letting them handle the burden of lessening the swag gap.

According to recent reports, aiyana Ishmael is the style editor at Cosmopolitan magazine. In her work, Aiyana focuses on the culture of fashion and how it intertwines and shapes the zeitgeist. She is an award-winning journalist from Miami, Florida, and a graduate of the historically Black university, Florida A&M. She is a 2024 Forbes 30 Under 30: Media honoree, and her debut romance novella PASSING GAME is set to release March of 2027 (831 Stories/Simon & Schuster).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Chalk it up to her era; Sade exploded in popularity in the ’80s, when these kinds of powerful silhouettes reigned supreme, but even beyond that, she knew the power of style.
  • Onstage, whether she was singing “Smooth Operator” or “No Ordinary Love,” she wore her finishing touches with pride: lush little leather gloves in olive green to match a soft-shouldered woolen suit, or a festooning delicate statement necklace layered over a black tank top.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Has there ever been anyone as effortlessly ahead of her time as Sade? Born Helen Folasade Adu on Jan. 16, 1959, in Ibadan, Nigeria, the frontwoman of her namesake band has a core aesthetic that revolves around blindingly bright hoop earrings, a slicked-back bun, a deep red lip, and strong yet minimal silhouettes. As the band is inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame this weekend, there’s never been a better time to reflect on the British-Nigerian singer’s personal style. Think: sweaters with strong shoulders, thick belts on long cinched skirts, and, when called for, a perfectly eccentric evening jacket souped up with embroidery and satisfyingly present buttons.

Chalk it up to her era; Sade exploded in popularity in the ’80s, when these kinds of powerful silhouettes reigned supreme, but even beyond that, she knew the power of style. And it’s no wonder: Years ago, in a rare radio interview, she divulged that fashion was her passion long before music. “I made clothes. For three years I went to an art college and did fashion at Central Saint Martins in London,” she remarked. “I actually sold clothes, and that’s when I started to sing. I had to make a choice between doing the two, because I didn’t have enough time.” Though her foray into design was incredibly sparsely documented, her focus was on menswear, and she later co-founded the tailored menswear fashion label Demob with designer Sarah Lee, where the duo created club-kid-ready attire.

Onstage, whether she was singing “Smooth Operator” or “No Ordinary Love,” she wore her finishing touches with pride: lush little leather gloves in olive green to match a soft-shouldered woolen suit, or a festooning delicate statement necklace layered over a black tank top. Rather than layer multiple pieces, she communicates through the subtle impact of one-and-done statements. A delicate stack of bracelets, or modernist front-facing Lucite hoop earrings, for instance. She usually leans into white and black, except for the rare occasion when she chooses a jammy, rich shade of plum or deep olive green. Her attention to detail does not go unnoticed; there’s a clear knack for tailored silhouettes.

Sade’s elusive nature combined with the ethereal sound of her music also contributes to fashion forming her memorable identity. Long before others made a plain turtleneck or slicked-back hairstyle their uniform, there was Sade doing it authentically, and with accessorized flair. And in today’s era of highly produced musicians who are styled by a team, Sade still stands out.

It has been revealed that though Sade and her band will not be present at the ceremony, they called it “both a gift and a timely reminder to give thanks, not only to those who voted for us but also every single person who lets our music into their lives” in a statement. For every person who’s ever loved an accessory and a bold shoulder look (especially gold hoop earrings), Sade’s presence lives on beyond the music too.

And while the official birthday celebration of the monarch falls in June with the annual Trooping the Colour military parade, the royal family marked his real date of birth with a upcoming portrait of him and Sir. Elton John.

Recent findings suggest that the photo was taken during the taping of a special edition of John’s Apple Music 1 radio show, Rocket Hour, in which the “Tiny Dancer” musician was joined by Charles to mark 50 years of the King’s Trust charity. And in addition to discussing the nonprofit, the two also chatted about modern music, introduced over a dozen hand-selected tracks, and joked about aging.

“We and the Trust are definitely still standing,” the king teased, highlighting the Grammy-winning singer’s “I’m Still Standing” as one of his favorite songs. The musician, from his seat at the table, replied, “I’m still sitting now, though.”.

At one point, the monarch gave a particular shoutout to Raye, who he stated he “had the pleasure of being introduced to” during a “very memorable performance” at Apple.

A key focus of the Rocket Hour podcast has been to champion emerging artists—a mission that resonates with the King’s Trust’s focus on supporting the next generation. Formerly known as the Prince’s Trust, the organization was founded in 1976 to help young people facing unemployment, homelessness, academic troubles, and more. John has celebrated the charity’s milestones before, even performing at Wembley Arena for the 10th anniversary (1986). In 2001, he joined the royal family for a 25th anniversary dinner at St. James’s Palace in London.

“We are so richly blessed with the talents of our musicians, singers, and performers, particularly yourself, if I may say so,” the king continued, turning to his host. “You’ve become such a national treasure.”.

After reporting another decline in U.S. sales, the fast food chain is testing changes to several of its best-known menu items. This refresh will appear on the menu at some point in 2027, according to Fox News.

According to recent reports, the most interesting update might be the Frosty, which Wendy's is working to make richer and creamier. The chain hasn't revealed the exact recipe changes, but given how recognizable the dessert has become, I'm curious how much the fresh version will differ. Whether or not it wins over fans who already know and love the original consistency is also up in the air.

It has been revealed that then there's the bacon. Wendy's is testing thicker, crispier bacon that could give sandwiches like the Baconator a more substantial bite. Personally, I think this is a pretty smart move. There's nothing more disappointing than ordering a bacon cheeseburger and barely noticing the bacon.

The chain is also experimenting with whole-leaf lettuce on sandwiches and upgraded salads, all part of an effort to improve the quality of its existing menu rather than relying entirely on fresh products.

Recent findings suggest that these changes aren’t coming out of nowhere. Wendy's reported a 5.7% decline in U.S. same-restaurant sales during the third quarter of 2026, marking another difficult period for the chain. In response, CEO Bob Wright is introducing a multi-year turnaround strategy called “Dave's Way,” named after Wendy's founder Dave Thomas.

Industry observers note that the strategy focuses on improving the menu, marketing, restaurant operations, and digital ordering experience while giving customers better value for their money. But depending on your nearest location, it might come at a cost: breakfast.

Wendy's is allowing franchise operators to decide whether offering breakfast makes financial sense for their individual restaurants. That means some locations could stop serving breakfast altogether, although the manufacturer isn't eliminating the morning menu nationwide.

Industry observers note that wendy's also plans to simplify its offerings by removing lower-selling items that make restaurant kitchens more complicated to operate. However, the chain hasn't provided a complete list of products that could disappear.

The chain is still testing upgraded ingredients, so we won’t know the extent of the menu refresh or when it’ll roll out until some point in 2027. But if you’re anything like me, you’ll be waiting with bated breath to see how Wendy’s changes one of the most iconic fast food desserts.

The 7 Best Electric Chainsaws of 2026

📅 11 Oct 2017 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you own a home with trees on your property, an electric chainsaw is a must-have tool in your yard care arsenal.
  • Sources indicate that saws with 24-inch bars or more are still considered gas engine territory, but that’s overkill for most homeowners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that if you own a home with trees on your property, an electric chainsaw is a must-have tool in your yard care arsenal. Electric chainsaws have come a long way and, in most cases, closed the gap to their gas-powered cousins—they’re easy to start (just push a button or two in most cases), generate little noise, produce no fumes, and simplify maintenance. We’ve tested electric saws as big as 20 inches and they’re powerful enough to bring down a mature tree.

Sources indicate that saws with 24-inch bars or more are still considered gas engine territory, but that’s overkill for most homeowners. For cleaning up after storms, felling small to medium-size trees, and regular pruning or arboreal maintenance, an electric chainsaw is the ideal choice.

We noted how well each chainsaw endured prolonged use. Making repeated cuts can cause a chainsaw, and its battery, to heat up. If it gets too hot, it will trigger a thermal limit and the saw’s overload protection will shut it down. We also considered comfort, vibration, saw balance, and ease of use to make our final recommendations.

Stihl’s new battery-powered MSA 260 C-O tops our list of chainsaws for two main reasons: run-time and constant, consistent power. These are the two most common concerns or complaints we hear from people when it comes to electric saws. The MSA 260 C-O made significantly more cuts on one battery charge than any other saw tested. But that’s only partly attributable to the saw—it’s also due to Stihl’s new AllPro 300.0 battery. Working in concert, the battery and saw deliver power at a constant level, maintaining a chain speed through most of the saw’s runtime.

Industry observers note that aside from run-time and consistent power delivery, the MSA 260 C-O has the ability to chew through big, tough logs. Note that Stihl positions the MSA 260 C-O “for professional applications” so the performance does come at a cost, $770 for the 18-inch model we tested, plus another $350 for the battery. While that might seem like a lot, it’s in line with other pro battery and gas saws. So, if you’re a frequent chainsaw user, the investment is going to be worth it.

Read Full Stihl MSA 260 C-O Review.

According to recent reports, the Power Axe also comes with a suite of well-designed, user-friendly features. The power button and boost button are located just above the handle so they’re easier to access on the fly. You also have the ability to adjust the chain tension by hand, loosening a dial to release the tension, then rotating a dial to tighten it back up. The whole process takes seconds. There’s also a built-in chain brake to protect from injuries. It’s a well-built, high-performing electric chainsaw that still manages to come in at a reasonable price.

Real the Full Husqvarna 350i Review.

Industry observers note that echo’s DCS-5000 gives you what you want most out of a chainsaw: raw cutting power. It may lack some of the bells and whistles you’ll find on pricier models, such as tool-less chain tensioning and power-saving settings, but its base performance is right up there with the Power Axe 350i. The DCS-5000 cut through 8-inch hardwood in less than 4 seconds. That's saying something considering that the DCS-5000 costs at least $100 less than any other saw that can do the same.

Sources indicate that along with its impressive cutting speed, the Echo is also relatively light at just over 12 pounds. I could feel the difference whenever I had to lift it up above shoulder-height to cut higher limbs, or while crouching down to cut a fallen 8-inch beech tree.

In a recent development, there is a trade-off with the DCS-5000, though, in that it lacks any kind of quality-of-life-related features. You won’t find tool-less chain tensioning or ECO settings that conserve battery life here. It’s pretty loud, too, producing 76 decibels at 60 feet. And, finally, while I appreciated the lighter weight, I could also feel the vibrations in my arm more than electric chainsaws with more refined builds.

Still, if you don't mind the rougher feel, higher noise level, and lack of a few user-friendly features you’ll find on pricier electric chainsaws, the Echo DCS-5000 offers exceptional value.

According to recent reports, the newest saw from Makita, the 40V Max XGT 20-inch chainsaw, is a beast. The brand claims it offers the power of a 50-cc gas saw, and we’re inclined to agree. The first pull of the trigger surprised us with the speed and sound of the chain whizzing around. And it wasn’t just the noise that was impressive—in testing, it positively tore through logs.

Sources indicate that using the 40V Max XGT for practical tasks like felling trees, or cleaning up fallen trees after a storm, confirmed its power. I tackled logs as massive as 18 inches, and the saw left nothing to be desired—it handled everything I used it on, without faltering. The 40V Max XGT chainsaw, at 20-inches, is among the biggest battery powered chainsaws we test. Our test unit came as a kit, with everything you need, including an 8.0Ah battery and charger. The kit isn’t cheap, but if you’re already on the Makita 40-volt XGT platform, you can save $500 and buy the chainsaw as a tool only.

Read Full Makita 40V Max XGT Review.

The Stihl MSA 80 is an easy-to-use chainsaw that also packs impressive cutting power. Its compact build—the 14-inch saw weighs about 10 pounds—gives it a balanced feel in hand. It features a narrow bar that makes it easier to fit it into the crotches of trees for pruning than other electric chainsaws we tested like the Ego 20-inch chainsaw or Husqvarna Power Axe 350i. Likewise, it comes equipped with a thinner chain that cuts more smoothly through wood, producing less vibration. Lastly, its variable speed trigger allows you to adjust the speed of the blade to suit the job at hand.

Sources indicate that there are several user-friendly features worth noting. Chain adjustments are effortless: Simply loosen a knob, turn the adjuster, and tighten the knob. There’s also a lubrication system to keep the chain moving with a minimal amount of bar oil.

Stihl’s chainsaws come at a premium price, and this one is no different. At $500, the MSA 80 is the most expensive electric chainsaw we tested, despite having a relatively short bar. Even so, it’s an ideal choice for homeowners who are looking for professional-grade build quality and performance out of an electric chainsaw.

If you already have other Echo tools, like a leaf blower or trimmer, then you can save a little cash and purchase the DCS-2500T as a tool only.

There’s a price for the CS-2005’s cutting power and capacity, though—its weight. While we liked its buttery smooth operation, it weighs an arm-burning 19.3 pounds with a battery. Making cuts on limbs above the head or below the knees was a far more challenging experience than with electric chainsaws we tested that were 4 to 5 pounds lighter. The Ego CS-2005 also lacks a tool-free chain tensioning system. If you don’t mind the extra heft, the Ego CS-2005 is the high-powered electric you’ll want for really substantial jobs.

As new models come out, we can’t keep all the models we test on our recommended list. But some of these older models and runners-up are still worth considering. Here are a few:.

In a recent development, milwaukee M18 Fuel 18V 16-Inch Electric Chainsaw: Don’t be fooled by the Milwaukee’s lower voltage, this saw has plenty of power for quickly cutting up large limbs or felling medium-sized trees. It’s a good saw, but we’d mostly recommend it to folks already on Milwaukee’s M18 platform, so you can buy it as a tool only and save some money.

According to recent reports, stihl GTA 26: While folks often refer to tools like this as “mini chain saws”, Stihl bills the GTA 26 as a garden pruner. Intended specifically for pruning shrubs and small branches, the GTA 26 combines light weight and a pistol-like configuration to make an easy-to-handle tool. Think of it as a power loppers, with greater size capability.

Worx Nitro WG385 40V 16-Inch Chainsaw: At less than $300, the Worx Nitro WG385 can get the job done. It’s lighter and easier to maneuver than other similarly sized saws, but it’s also a little less powerful, with a little less run-time. Still, with some patience we were able to find it useful for basic property maintenance. For the price, the Worx Nitro WG385 is a good cost-effective option for occasional use.

It has been revealed that at the heart of an electric chainsaw is its motor and battery, which need to work in concert to perform well. The longer the chainsaw bar, the bigger the log or tree you can cut. So, the motor has to have enough torque and speed, while the battery has to be able to deliver the power needed to sustain that torque and speed. This is one reason why bigger saws can cost a lot more than smaller ones. Batteries are a significant factor in the price of a saw, and bigger batteries cost more. Battery size is typically measured in amp-hours (Ah), and larger saws will typically have 8 to 12 Ah batteries.

Mini chainsaws, made for pruning and other small jobs, feature a one-handed design with a small cutting bar—4 to 8 inches—and a small battery. If you need to break down large branches from trees, opt for a smaller full-size chainsaw with a 12- to 14-inch cutting bar. For something professional-grade, consider a large chainsaw with a 16- to 20-inch cutting bar and larger battery.

Among electric chainsaws with comparable bar lengths, those with larger batteries will typically have more ripping power, which means they’ll cut through limbs and logs more quickly, allowing you to get the job done faster. Just keep in mind that a more powerful chainsaw is also often a heavier chainsaw.

An electric chainsaw’s runtime depends on the capacity of its battery, in amp-hours. Broadly speaking, more capacity means more juice, but larger saws draw more power per second, so it’s not uncommon to find large chainsaws with large batteries getting comparable battery life to their smaller, more efficient counterparts.

In a recent development, since your chainsaw only uses power when you’re using it to cut, its true runtime comes down to how many cuts it can make on a single charge. The Popular Mechanics test team tests runtime by checking how many times each model cuts through a 6-inch log on a single charge. Depending on battery size and chainsaw power, that number can vary quite a bit—from as low as 50 to as high as 300.

The “cutting bar” is the business end of the chainsaw—the long, rounded metal guide that the chain spins around to create a blade. The length of the bar, which is measured from the base of the chainsaw’s head to the tip of the cutting bar, determines the maximum thickness of the wood that your chainsaw can cut through in a single pass. Generally speaking, your chainsaw can safely cut through limbs with a diameter up to 2 inches less than the length of the bar. For example, a 12-inch chainsaw can cut through a limb up to 10 inches in diameter in a single pass.

According to recent reports, for a long time, going electric meant settling for a chainsaw with a shorter bar, but that’s no longer the case. While gas engines offer more power, especially in larger saws, there are electric options with professional-length cutting bars. For instance, a 20-inch electric chainsaw has the power to bring down mature trees.

Industry observers note that need is an key distinction here. We don’t recommend picking the most powerful saw with the longest cutting bar within your budget. A longer bar will give you more cutting capacity, but it’s also heavier and more difficult to handle safely. We recommend buying the tool that’s just big enough for the cutting tasks you’ll perform regularly. If you’re looking to trim small limbs and branches, a pruning saw with a 4- to 8-inch bar such as the Stihl GTA 26 is going to be the best choice. If you’re taking down trees and breaking them down for firewood, you may need something longer.

It’s notable that you feel comfortable handling the weight of your chainsaw. If it’s too heavy to hold at chest height, then you can’t use it safely.

It has been revealed that with electric chainsaws, weight is directly related to the length of the cutting bar. The longer the cutting bar, the heavier the chainsaw. A mini chainsaw with an 8-inch bar will weigh around 5 pounds, while a large 18-inch chainsaw can weigh as much as 15 pounds.

One thing to keep in mind: Many manufacturers list the “bare” weight of their cordless chainsaws without the battery, so when you do add that in, it can mean an extra 1 to 3 pounds to the load.

Chainsaws are among the most dangerous power tools you can put your hands on: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), some 36,000 people ends up in the hospital with chainsaw-related injuries each year.

That is why it’s crucial to always take every step you can to ensure the safest possible conditions when using a chainsaw. A good electric chainsaw should have built-in safety features to minimize the possibility of an accident: First, look for a trigger lock, which requires you to maintain pressure on a button near the handle to keep the chain spinning. Most will also have a chain brake at the front of the handle, which disengages the chain if the chainsaw kicks back.

Sources indicate that that depends on the size of the tree. Even the largest electric chainsaws with a 20-inch cutting bar only have the torque necessary to cut down moderately tall trees. You’ll want a gas chainsaw that brings the extra power to bring down an older, larger tree, or if you’re bringing trees down regularly.

Electric chainsaws don’t require much maintenance. Use a brush or cloth to remove sawdust and other debris that’s caught in the chain and sprocket area after each use.

You should also clean any debris that’s fallen into the air intake slots: Brush it away material on the outside with a clean paintbrush, then blow the valves out with compressed air.

Lastly, electric chainsaws have an auto-lubrication mechanism, but we recommend checking the chain oil reservoir before each use, and refilling it if necessary.

It has been revealed that many cordless electric chainsaws are water resistant and will work fine in the rain. Before you take one for a spin, check its Ingress Protection rating (IP), which measures dust and waterproofing. If your chainsaw features an “IPX3” rating, it can handle “sprays of water” and should be fine in light rain. An “IPX4” rating can withstand moderate to heavy rain.

Recent findings suggest that all that noted, we don’t really recommend operating a chainsaw in the rain. Even with work gloves, rain makes every chainsaw-related job less safe, so hold off until the sun comes out if you can.

In a recent development, you should never use a corded electric chainsaw in the rain. Doing so presents a significant electrocution risk. (It’s one of many reasons we generally don’t recommend them.).

In a recent development, every year, the Baby2Baby Gala brings together the biggest names in philanthropy, entertainment, and fashion for an evening of fundraising and celebration. And last night, the 15th edition was no exception—with the likes of Demi Moore, Andrew Garfield, Jessica Alba, Barbara Palvin and Dylan Sprouse, Kerry Washington, and Katy Perry showing up in West Hollywood to support the organization’s mission to help kids in need.

According to recent reports, from the gala’s inception, Baby2Baby co-CEOS Norah Weinstein and Kelly Sawyer Patricof wanted to create an event that felt “less like a traditional fundraiser.” Year after year, the night has offered its star-studded guests more than just an excuse to get dressed up and a chance to make a difference with their wallets—pairing fundraising efforts with exclusive dining experiences from top chefs and intimate performances from award-winning musicians. (Last night, Carbone flew in from New York City and Cardi B took the stage.).

Industry observers note that “We wanted to create an event that would appeal to a younger generation of donors through our approach to food, fashion, and celebrity, while making sure that nobody left the gala without understanding our mission,” Weinstein and Patricof told Harper’s Bazaar. “Fifteen years later, the gala has evolved in ways we never could have imagined, but some themes have stayed exactly the same. Every flower and fork is underwritten by our generous sponsors so that every dollar raised can go directly to Baby2Baby and the children we serve.”.

In a recent development, each year, the funds raised from the gala help get millions of basic essentials—from diapers to formula to clothing—to children who need them. But the organization, with an all-female board of directors, spends all year working towards the Baby2Baby mission. “The gala brings this extraordinary community together for one night, but it’s their commitment throughout the year that makes our work possible,” the CEOs shared.

Breaking: Laila Gohar Is Inspiring Us to Celebrate Our Own Made-Up Holidays

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • It has been revealed that on Avenue George V in Paris, in the lobby of the Hotel Prince de Galles, is a festive installation that looks straight out of a Wes Anderson movie.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It has been revealed that on Avenue George V in Paris, in the lobby of the Hotel Prince de Galles, is a festive installation that looks straight out of a Wes Anderson movie. It’s a pop-up fashioned to look like the counter of a vintage apothecary, with rows of cup-handled drawers lining a dark wooden wall, each numbered and labeled, with an attendant standing in front in a dark green uniform and cap. Flanking it on both sides are glass casings with Christmas trees—made from light-blue fabric and white ribbons—inside, surrounded by metallic ant figurines.

Recent findings suggest that the whimsical, imaginative display is part of artist Laila Gohar’s ongoing collaboration with The Luxury Collection, the hotel group, which boasts the Prince de Galles as one of its many properties. For the holidays, Gohar curated an advent calendar with each of its 24 windows offering a peek into a different hotel in the collection, from Madrid, Kyoto, Dubai, and more. In a way, this Parisian pop-up, with set designs by Alix Bortoli, is a life-size extension of the work. Similar versions appear in The Joseph in Nashville, Tennessee, Solaz in Los Cabos, and The Laurus in Singapore.

It has been revealed that gohar tapped her artistic circle for the project. “When people ask me, ‘Who inspires you?’ my answer is always my friends,” she claims. The advent calendar’s exterior is illustrated by Upcoming York-based Joana Avillez and fashioned to look like a hotel out of a storybook. (It’s not based on any particular one in real life, though.) “When you open it up, inside of the flaps, there are all these little vignettes,” Gohar explains to ELLE. “It’s like all these imagined little scenarios, and some of them have a little bit of humor, but it’s a little bit of a Where’s Waldo thing. It’s also kind of in the style of Richard Scarry. Do you remember those books from childhood?”.

Inside each window is a chocolate from Casa Bosques—founded by designer Rafael Prieto, another one of Gohar’s pals—featuring flavors from each destination. “For example, for The Suiran in Kyoto, the chocolate featured inside has black sesame and other flavors associated with Japan and with that city,” Gohar explains.

It’s a fitting undertaking for Gohar, who first earned renown for works of art made with food and has since developed her own design studio, Gohar World. (The brand just opened up a shop on Elizabeth Street in New York.) “While I care very much about food, for me, it’s more about creating a particular feeling in a space, and that can be through lots of different mediums,” she says.

According to recent reports, that medium could be an advent calendar full of chocolates or a historic Art Deco hotel like the Prince de Galles, with its majestic marble details and mosaic tiles. ELLE caught up with Gohar one morning in Paris to discuss her latest projects, holiday gifting, and her hosting tips.

In a recent development, yeah. I think there’s something nostalgic about advent calendars and you have something to look forward to every day. What I like about it is that there’s all this excitement around it, but you also have to practice a little restraint, which as a kid, I don’t know if I really did. I would blast through all of them. My mom was like, “You have to wait!” I think a lot of people grew up with them, but adults love them too. It’s very giftable, which I thought would be good for the holidays.

In a recent development, I love to give gifts that feel almost like an heirloom, like something that was maybe in your family. Especially with my friends, we think about that a lot. What are we creating that can be passed down from generation to generation? What is something that is really considered, that took a lot of time to create? I love thinking about gifts through that lens.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot of pressure around giving gifts for the holidays, and obviously the way we shop now is very online. So I like to create things that feel a little bit slower and more craft-based.

It has been revealed that for the holidays, or just in general, I always say that people are only able to relax and have a good time in your home or around you if you’re relaxed and having a good time. I think that’s really what it comes down to. You have to set yourself up for success, and that means you’re not getting involved with a really difficult cooking project that you’re really nervous about—you’re going to be running the stove all the time. That is not good. Just figure out how to create an environment that feels relaxing for you, and therefore everyone will relax and hopefully have a good time.

Oh my God, I’ve hosted so many. I write a column for The Financial Times, “How to Spend It,” and the premise of it is made-up holidays, because I just like the idea of thinking of a random excuse to get people together. I think there’s a lot of pressure around the holidays, but I like just celebrating random everyday things. For example, throwing a party because I saw really beautiful dahlias in the market and I think we should have a dahlia party. We’re going to have a soup party because it’s the coldest night of the year, or we will have a potato party because there are new potatoes in the market and I love potatoes.

It has been revealed that yeah. All of those are real ones. They’re not hypothetical. And I’ve done a million random things that I just kind of make up. I think there’s a reason to celebrate obviously around the holidays, but also every day. If you take a minute, there’s always a reason to spread joy and a reason to celebrate.

Last week, I was in Dakar, Senegal, and I’m participating in a biennial that’s happening there soon. In Senegal, people have unbelievable style, and you see it in just how they carry themselves and how they put outfits together. They just have this swag, and I think it makes for really great people-watching. I was inspired by people’s sense of self and how they move, how they carry themselves, how confident they appear.

It’s for the Dakar Biennale, which is the most significant art biennial in Africa. I’m from Egypt, so it was really important for me to be there. For the project, I’ve created a tapestry carpet—it’s kind of like a quilt. I teamed up with a friend of mine, Rym Beydoun; she has a clothing brand called Super Yaya. Together we created this textile that transforms a room in the biennial into a meditation space. It’s inspired vaguely by prayer carpets. Senegal is a Muslim country, and there are a lot of different carpets there, but also all over the Muslim world.

We created 25 unique carpets in the prayer carpet size, which is small, and then we sewed them all together to create this really big composition. The idea was to create a little space of refuge. The biennial’s in this big, beautiful building, and we just wanted this little corner where people could just sit with themselves for a second and spend a little time with themselves.

I think there’s inspiration everywhere you look. It depends on how you look. But I love to notice beauty or inspiration in the least expected places. Obviously there’s tons of inspiration in museums and in films and all that, but I like to notice random accidental beauty. I’m a little embarrassed to admit this, but a thing that I do is when I’m sitting on the train in New York, I kind of look at every person and I try to find one thing that I think is beautiful about them.

Industry observers note that it’s a fun way to pass time. I see an old man sitting on the train, and I’m like, “His hair is really good,” or something. You notice all sorts of crazy things that you never would [if you didn’t] look at the person that way.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

What’s the Best Snow and Ice Melt? Here’s Why Using Rock Salt Shouldn’t Be Your Default Option.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that if the winter weather in recent years hasn’t already been causing some chaos, this year’s Super El Niño isn’t helping.
  • According to recent reports, not all ice melt is created equal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that if the winter weather in recent years hasn’t already been causing some chaos, this year’s Super El Niño isn’t helping. Preparation is key. Setting down a layer of snow and ice melt (i.e., deicers) on your driveway and walkways before a snowstorm hits can save you a lot of time shoveling or snow blowing. But when you walk into the home improvement store, there might be more options than you were prepared for. Don’t worry, with just a little bit of information under your belt, you can choose the best ice melt for the job.

According to recent reports, not all ice melt is created equal. Some melts don’t work as well as others in subzero temperatures and won’t be effective against bonded ice. And some ice melt negatively affects nearby lawns and plants, or causes irritation and health problems for pets. Knowing the difference between the ingredients that power your snow and ice melts is important when choosing the right one for you.

Recent findings suggest that deicers work by exhibiting one of two thermal reactions: exothermic or endothermic. Exothermic materials, such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride, release heat when they come into contact with ice or snow. Endothermic materials, such as rock salt and calcium magnesium acetate, absorb heat from their surroundings (such as the sun) and use that heat to melt ice.

According to recent reports, because of this difference, exothermic ice melts perform better in subzero temperatures, and endothermic melts become less effective below 20 degrees Fahrenheit or so, especially at night. However, though exothermic reactions are stronger, they can also be more corrosive and less friendly to plants and animals. Blended melts may offer a good balance, which can help the melt work better in lower temperatures, but also be less corrosive and harmful to pets and plants.

Sometimes referred to as a deicer and often simply called “salt,” ice and snow melts can be made of different chemical compounds or blended to take advantage of their different attributes. This can make some less damaging to pavements or nearby plants. We put together a list of the most typical compounds that you’ll see sold by themselves or in a list of ingredients in blended options, which are the most common types you’ll see at stores.

Recent findings suggest that these are some of the most common types of compounds used for melting ice and snow. Some are sold in their pure form or may be an ingredient in a blended formula.

Exothermic ice melt compounds, such as calcium chloride and magnesium chloride, work better in subzero temperatures because they release heat. If you live in an area where winter temperatures regularly drop below zero, consider one of these types or a blend that contains them.

If your winters are milder and average temperatures tend to hover in the twenties, an endothermic ice melt like rock salt or a urea blend can get the job done. Blended ice melts will often combine exothermic and endothermic compounds to help them perform better in lower temperatures and keep the cost more reasonable. Companies that make these blends will often label the bag with the lowest effective temperature to help you know for sure.

Sources indicate that traditional salts can irritate dog and cat paws, and some of the stronger exothermic compounds that include chlorides can also be irritating or harmful if ingested. The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) says ingestion can lead to ice melt toxicosis, which can cause vomiting or neurological problems. However, ice melt toxicosis is unlikely to happen from just a few licks; the most serious cause is when a bag of melt is left unattended and ingested by your pet in large amounts.

Recent findings suggest that to help combat this, many brands offer “pet safe” varieties of ice melt, but no blend is truly perfect. These animal-friendly blends tend to eliminate sodium or chloride from the mix, but not all do. The ASPCA recommends using urea-based ice melts, as urea (a compound made of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen) is the least likely ingredient to cause stomach irritation. Another simple idea, especially in cities and suburbs where there is little control over what ice melt the neighbors use, is to adorn your dog in paw booties before taking a walk.

Recent findings suggest that ice melts that have high concentrations of salts or chlorides can be problematic for vegetation and the environment in general. According to a study by Penn State Extension, when used in large amounts, simple rock salt (sodium chloride) can injure or kill plants near the treated pavement as it washes away, and further pollute waterways, harming fish and other marine life. Instead, the study notes, a compound like calcium magnesium acetate (CMA), which forgoes the use of chlorides or salts, is a safer option for environmentally sensitive areas. Urea-based ice melts are also a good choice.

Like the pet-friendly varieties of deicers, brands can be very loose with how they market their eco-friendly products, especially with the blends; there’s no guarantee that the one you buy won’t partially contain a compound that is harmful in large quantities. If you want to be as eco-friendly as possible, avoid blends that include chlorides and salts.

According to recent reports, if that can’t be avoided, just follow the golden rule of “everything in moderation.” After all, overtreating an area is more likely to damage nearby vegetation—even if you use the more environmentally friendly varieties. If you’re still finding noticeable piles of deicer after the snow and ice are gone, you might be using too much.

Corrosion is a considerable problem caused by deicers. Salt-based melts or brines can penetrate porous stone, freeze, and cause the surface to expand. Meanwhile, chlorides can accelerate the rate of corrosion in metal. The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency noted that acetate-based deicers that don’t use chlorides or salts caused low to moderate levels of corrosion, but again, using any ice melt in moderation will help lower the chance of corrosion to your sidewalks, driveways, and nearby railings.
