  • If you’ve watched the original film series, then you already know.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the immortal words of Cornelius Fudge, “He’s back.”.

Fifteen years after young wizard Harry Potter last appeared in the film Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 2—and no matter how much vitriol has followed—Warner Bros. Discovery has summoned another incarnation of the Wizarding World saga. But there’s a twist! This time, the story will take the form of a seven-season television series (rather than an eight-film franchise) and will span a full decade. And there’s more! A upcoming cast will fill the old roles made famous by the likes of Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, Emma Watson, and co.

Here’s a quick breakdown of what we know so far.

If you’ve watched the original film series, then you already know. Zaslav has promised that the reboot will be a faithful adaptation of the seven books in author J.K. Rowling’s series—meaning it will tell the exact same story as the movies, though with greater detail. Each season of the HBO series will cover the material in one of the books, so we can expect seven seasons in total.

Sources indicate that here’s how HBO Max is describing the series: “The stories from each of Rowling’s Harry Potter books will become a decade-long series produced with the same epic craft, love and care this global franchise is known for. The series will feature a fresh cast to lead a new generation of fandom, full of the fantastic detail, much loved characters and dramatic locations that Harry Potter fans have loved for over 25 years. Each season will be authentic to the original books and bring Harry Potter and these incredible adventures to new audiences around the world, while the original, classic and beloved films will remain at the core of the franchise and available to watch globally.”.

According to recent reports, the cast is “fresh,” meaning—thankfully—Radcliffe and friends won’t be expected to undergo any CGI de-aging. Instead, the roles they made famous will go to newcomers Dominic McLaughlin (as Harry Potter), Arabella Stanton (as Hermione Granger), and Alastair Stout (as Ron Weasley).

Recent findings suggest that of the hunt for these actors, showrunner/executive producer Francesca Gardiner and director/executive producer Mark Mylod released the following statement in May 2025: “After an extraordinary search led by casting directors Lucy Bevan and Emily Brockmann, we are delighted to announce we have found our Harry, Hermione, and Ron. The talent of these three unique actors is wonderful to behold, and we cannot wait for the world to witness their magic together onscreen. We would like to thank all the tens of thousands of children who auditioned. It’s been a real pleasure to discover the plethora of young talent out there.”.

The announcement of these latest lead actors followed multiple other rounds of casting reveals, starting in April 2025. The manufacturer first shared the identities of four adult actors, three of whom had already been reported by Variety and Deadline. They were as follows:.

HBO also confirmed the cast for two smaller but nevertheless essential roles:.

On June 9, 2025, nine more cast members were added to the ensemble:.

On July 14, 2025, another round of cast members was unveiled:.

On August 19, 2025, the upcoming members of the Weasley family were revealed:.

On October 27, HBO revealed more roles:.

On October 30, Deadline revealed the addition of five more members to the season 1 cast:.

Gardiner and Mylod, who have each worked on Succession, were enlisted for the new series, Variety first reported in June 2024. They are both serving as executive producers, along with Rowling, Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them’s Neil Blair, Brontë Film and TV’s Ruth Kenley-Letts, and David Heyman of Heyday Films. Gardiner will also be the writer and showrunner, while Mylod directed some episodes. In addition, Killing Eve writer Laura Neal joined the writers’ room.

Sources indicate that the Harry Potter series is confirmed to release its first season—titled, appropriately, Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone—on Dec. 25, 2026, on HBO and HBO Max.

According to recent reports, yes. On March 25, 2026, HBO Max released the first official teaser for the upcoming series. Watch it below.

In a recent development, A second teaser trailer arrived on September 2, giving fans a better look inside life at Hogwarts. The clip opens with the Sorting Hat Ceremony in the Great Hall before the start-of-term banquet. Harry begs the Sorting Hat to not put him in Slytherin, leading to his Gryffindor placement (and a warm welcome from the rest of his housemates).

It has been revealed that “Mr. Potter, I expect you to work hard. Find what sparks your interests, and make solid friendships,” Professor McGonagall tells Harry during a meeting in her office, which is spliced between scenes of him receiving his class schedule and finding the humor in Herbology class. But it isn’t an easy transition for The Boy Who Lived—he struggles in Charms classes, leading to his first set of insecurities. “Everyone thinks I’m this great wizard, but I really don’t know anything,” he states.

According to recent reports, harry later hits his stride as a Quidditch star, giving fans of the franchise a look inside the game as the famous boy wizard chases the golden snitch in the hopes of winning the match. Fans will also recognize The Burrow, Wizards Chess game, and the scary moment when the trio encounters Fluffy.

On Nov. 14, 2026, HBO released the first full scene from its upcoming Harry Potter series, offering a new look at the Hogwarts start-of-term banquet. The 90-second clip follows Harry, Ron, and Hermione as they attend their first feast in the Great Hall after the Sorting Ceremony.

The scene opens with students chanting for headmaster Albus Dumbledore, before Harry asks Ron whether Dumbledore is “a bit mad.” Ron replies, “Yep, totally off his rocker.” Dumbledore then magically conjures the banquet with a snap of his fingers.

The footage also includes a conversation between Dumbledore and Professor Minerva McGonagall about Harry’s placement in Gryffindor. McGonagall remarks on how much Harry resembles his father, James Potter, prompting Dumbledore to remind her, “Looks can be deceiving, Minerva. His nature is entirely his own.”.

Industry observers note that although fans would love to see the original members make a cameo in the remake, Radcliffe told ComicBook.com in July 2023 that he won’t be pursuing an opportunity to be in the show. “My understanding is that they’re trying to very much start fresh, and I’m sure whoever is making them will want to make their own mark on it and probably not want to have to figure out how to get old Harry to cameo in this somewhere,” he said. “So I’m definitely not seeking it out in any way. But I do wish them, obviously, all the luck in the world, and I’m very excited to have that torch passed. But I don’t think it needs me to physically pass it.”.

Radcliffe also told ScreenRant in February 2026 that he wants the young actors in the newly introduced series to be given a chance to succeed on their own terms.

“When these kids got cast, there was a whole thing around the internet [with] people saying we have to ‘look after these kids,’” he told the outlet, when asked what advice he’d give the upcoming actors. “If everyone really means that one of the things you can do for me is not ask about us—me, Emma [Watson], Rupert [Grint]—all the time,” he added. “I would like not to be a weird spectral phantom in these children’s lives and just to let them get on because it’s going to be a new thing and it’s going to be a different thing.”.

Without digging too deep into the Discourse™️, we can summarize two main reasons why some audiences aren’t convinced a Harry Potter reboot is, shall we say, necessary:.

It has been revealed that one is that Rowling will be involved not only as the source material’s creator but as an executive producer, meaning she’ll have some creative control over the reboot and will, of course, benefit financially from its success. That’s not good news for many fans who consider her controversial history of trans-exclusionary feminism to be a rot in an otherwise beloved franchise.

It has been revealed that the second is that the story is far from new, nor is it particularly old. Harry Potter is practically inescapable in modern life. Whether it’s his books or his films or his merchandise or his theme parks or his exhibits or his video games, the boy with the lightning bolt scar is astoundingly difficult to avoid. A certain air of exhaustion (not to mention anger) has permeated even the most devoted corners of the Wizarding World fan base. What more can really be squeezed out of not just the same franchise, but the same story? Still, as time has passed since the announcement, it would seem more and more fans have come around to the idea of a Harry Potter adaptation that is deeply and thoroughly faithful to the books. As one commenter on the teaser trailer put it, “This is what I have always wanted. The books fleshed out in [a] TV series. No movie can do justice to how much there is in the books.”.

Addressing the conversation around Rowling herself in a presentation timed to the series’ initial announcement, Casey Bloys, chairman and CEO of HBO & Max Content, had only this to add: “J.K. is an executive producer, and her insights will be helpful. We are in the Harry Potter business. The TV show is new and exciting, but we’ve been in the Harry Potter business for 20 years; this isn’t a new decision. We’re comfortable being in the Potter business. J.K. is a very online conversation…it’s very nuanced and complicated and not something we’re going to get into. Our priority is what’s onscreen. The Harry Potter story is incredibly affirmative and positive about love and acceptance, and that’s our priority, what’s on the screen.”.

Sources indicate that go to any high-end hotel or luxury chain gym these days and you’ll see a NordicTrack treadmill with a massive screen, a fancy rowing machine, and maybe a shallow pool for a cold plunge. You also may see a glowing red box in place of the traditional steam room. That’s an infrared sauna, and it’s at the cutting edge of wellness tech. At the end of the day, nothing compares to sweating it out.

Before you tell me it’s not feasible or you don’t have the space or don’t want to tear up a wall, hear me out. Plenty of people have saunas in their homes. And with an infrared sauna, the process doesn’t require complicated plumbing and ventilation. Instead, it’s all electric and easier than ever to set up in your home. Instead of traditional water-based saunas, infrared saunas use infrared light to heat you. The ambient temperature won’t get as hot as steam-based saunas, but the far-infrared light will penetrate your body directly. In short, it won’t feel as hot and you’ll still sweat.

In a recent development, for all these reasons, infrared saunas started to catch on as a home alternative to spending an extra half hour at your gym or going to the bathhouse. Many of them can fit more than one person, but you can opt for something a bit more snug as well. Some of them even have Bluetooth speakers. We’ve even found an option for those who truly don’t have the space. Call it an apartment-friendly solution. No matter your needs or restrictions, these are the best infrared saunas for your home.

It has been revealed that first and foremost, the LIT Method BeautyBox is just a great sauna. No buts or caveats, it was good enough that we called it the best home sauna of 2026 in this year’s gadget awards. It uses the full spectrum of infrared (near, mid, and far), which adds a broader range of health benefits. Far-infrared is what causes the sweating, but the often left out mid and near wavelengths penetrate your skin and blood vessels for more comprehensive relaxation and recovery.

Recent findings suggest that the BeautyBox comfortably fits two people. It’s crafted with care from Canadian hemlock and non-toxic adhesives, so you don’t worry about heating up microplastics and absorbing that into your skin. Esquire executive editor, Madison Vain, had the BeautyBox installed in her basement and it’s since become a major part of her routine.

In a recent development, “I cannot prove that my LIT BeautyBox kept me any healthier than, say, 30-minute meditation sessions or a regular wine date with friends,” she wrote. “But meditation doesn’t make you sweat, and as good as they say socializing is for the body, I think we can all assume heat therapy does a bit more. Sources indicate that if you ask around on Reddit and the other places where (non-bot) people still hang out, Sun Home makes the best infrared saunas. You’ll get better coverage from full-spectrum, but the amount of heat and sweat should be about the same either way, since that’s coming from the far-infrared.

According to recent reports, the Solstice 1 only seats one, but you can pay more for larger versions, with the largest having the capacity for four people with the Solstice 4. Whichever you pick, they are all made from eucalyptus and low-VOC (volatile organic compound) materials. And they all come with speakers installed that you can connect your phone to via Bluetooth and stream in your favorite Spotify playlists.

According to recent reports, if you’re a DIY king, or live with one, you might just want to order something from Amazon; this is the most popular and well-reviewed option. Robert Pattinson Will Make a Bold, Dangerous, and Entirely Original 007

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that james Bond’s greatest weakness is not megalomaniacal madmen bent on world domination.
  • That’s why Robert Pattinson’s casting as filmmaker Denis Villeneuve’s new 007 is a bold and promising choice.
  • Sources indicate that some things shouldn’t change, like his seductiveness, the Walther PPK, and the way he likes his martinis to be shaken.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that james Bond’s greatest weakness is not megalomaniacal madmen bent on world domination. Those, he can handle. The superspy is far more likely to be taken down by well-meaning committees.

That’s why Robert Pattinson’s casting as filmmaker Denis Villeneuve’s new 007 is a bold and promising choice. The two of them together have amassed enough industry clout to craft the character their own way, to make him distinctive and daring in a way, hopefully, that we haven’t seen before.

Sources indicate that some things shouldn’t change, like his seductiveness, the Walther PPK, and the way he likes his martinis to be shaken. But those things only make up the silhouette of James Bond. Each actor must put his own imprint on the core of Ian Fleming’s debonair secret agent, just as the author did in his original novels. Sean Connery added ruggedness to the savoir faire. George Lazenby gave him a soulful vulnerability in his solo outing as the character. Roger Moore sharpened 007’s sense of humor. Each actor leaves his fingerprints behind as he hands it off to the next.

This leads to the essential question for anyone signing up to play James Bond: Are you strong enough to stand out?

It’s not so easily answered. I’ll let Timothy Dalton, my personal favorite Bond, explain: “I have some good friends from the Bond days, some really good people, but they’re trapped. Everyone’s trapped by it in a way,” he told me. “Whoever does it has got to have a very clear sense of what they want to achieve, because everybody in the world has got a different opinion about it.”.

To figure out what comes next, we should look back at what came before.

Dalton (who also happens to be Christopher Nolan’s favorite Bond too) made that comment to me back in February 2025, when Amazon MGM Studios first acquired the rights to the 007 character.

Sources indicate that when he first took on the role in 1987’s The Living Daylights, his choice was to add a renegade wolf quality. But he also recognized that James Bond must remain, ultimately, the good guy, and that movie was entirely defined by an act of mercy. Fleming’s “The Living Daylights” short story makes up the film’s opening scene: Bond has been sent to take out an enemy sniper, but when he sees that his target is a beautiful cellist (played by Maryam d'Abo), he aims his own rifle to distract her rather than kill her.

It has been revealed that he then becomes responsible for her life, and his 007 has no problem cutting down any foes who block their paths. Dalton’s Bond was more polished than Connery, and less comedic than Moore, but he was led by a kind of stormy passion. He had heart, but it pumped cold blood.

Still, Dalton had to break through that formidable wall of consensus. Bond is not a solo enterprise, of course. The director has a say, as do the producers, and the screenwriters, but the danger comes from two places: the studio and the audience itself. As Dalton noted, “everybody in the world has got a different opinion about it,” and those voices have to be defied, just as his 007 refused the order to place a bullet in the enemy cellist’s heart.

Nothing makes hands wring and sweat pour in a studio conference room like something unexpected, and know-it-all supposed “fans” often resist change while paradoxically demanding something fresh and fresh. He had two outings as Bond, the second being 1989’s License to Kill, in which 007 goes even more rogue, defying Her Majesty’s secret service to embark on a mission of revenge. Then the character became tied up in rights lawsuits for several years, and Dalton chose not to return.

When Daniel Craig took over 007 from Pierce Brosnan in 2005, purists complained about his blue eyes and blond hair. When they finally saw him bring the character to life in 2006’s Casino Royale, those critics soon fell silent. Craig gave Bond a soldier’s mindset. He was a battlefield veteran whose new uniform happens to be a dashing suit. He was successful for so long because as he added his own spin, he capitalized on the best of what came before: he was as rough as Connery and as lethal as Dalton. The humor and playfulness that defined Moore and Brosnan were still present, but they served as a mask for the kind of wounded vulnerability that Lazenby had introduced.

Pattinson is now free to pick and choose whatever qualities he likes from this Brotherhood of Bond, but if he is going to take anyone’s advice, it should be Dalton’s: “Whoever does it has got to have a very clear sense of what they want to achieve.”.

It has been revealed that fortunately, no one tells Villeneuve what to do. The filmmaker has spent two decades establishing himself not just as a distinctive artist, but as a reliable box-office draw. Those two qualities give him a powerful weapon—clout—that can stave off the onslaught of opinions that will inevitably surround this casting choice.

Just this Saturday, I moderated a Q&A with Villeneuve at the Golden Globes Foundation before an audience of students, and one young filmmaker named Oscar Flores asked the Dune filmmaker: “When is the right time for you to listen to feedback, and when is the right time to listen to yourself?”.

According to recent reports, villeneuve gave an answer that perfectly matches Dalton’s advice and increases my optimism about his approach to Bond: “Honestly, people say that I’m humble, but that’s bullshit,” he stated, only partly joking. “If I'm asking for $200 million for a movie, what kind of humility is that?”.

The suggestion he made to the students was to not take on projects that are outside their control. Start small, stay true, and build up your skill set behind the camera while establishing a reputation that gives you defining power over the movies you make. He warned them not to follow the “siren” song of a big-budget offer if it means ceding control. Instead, Villeneuve remarked, he found it effective to build up his status with smaller films, moving from the more intimate 2010’s Incendies to 2013’s harrowing Prisoners and 2015’s even more sprawling Sicario before leveling up in scale to 2016’s Arrival and 2017’s Blade Runner 2049.

In a recent development, “The thing that I did when I was a young filmmaker is that I tried not to jump steps,” he told us at the Golden Globes Foundation forum. “I went step by step on projects. I was able to keep control of them. I was making sure that I was in control of the tools, and control of the language, and getting strong with the crew, being able to and making sure that my voice would be heard. … What I will say to you is: be careful of the sirens.”.

In a recent development, only after amassing this authority, Villeneuve noted, did he feel the time was right to take on his dream project of Dune. “If you made a successful first feature film that cost $200,000 and they offer you a major blockbuster, be careful,” he said this weekend. “Be careful who you are working with and don't listen to your ego. Do you really believe that you have the skills to bring it to the screen? Maybe you do. Some people can by the way. I was not ready to make Dune after my second [film] ... It took me a lot of movies before I knew that I was able to handle the pressure and making sure that I would be able to control totally, 100 percent, the film. At the end of the day when I look at the movie and the screen, it's my movie.”.

Recent findings suggest that no doubt, Pattinson’s casting was his decision, and Villeneuve’s status ensured it was accepted by the powers that be at Amazon MGM Studios. It probably wasn’t a difficult yes, given that Pattinson is currently in his prime. Not only is he The Batman, but he stood out as the conniving usurper Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, and he has earned accolades for his haunting performance as a predator-hunting journalist in Primetime.

According to recent reports, is he a heartthrob? Ask the legion of Twilight fans, and cover your ears for their deafening reply.

In a recent development, pattinson forged his bond with Villeneuve with another upcoming role in Dune: Part Three, playing the Face Dancer Scytale. He’s a shapeshifting psychological assassin who seeks to undermine Timothée Chalamet’s all-seeing, all-powerful emperor by getting inside his head, and the actor and filmmaker worked closely to figure out the look, mannerisms, and motivations of a creature void of form.

In a recent development, as Pattinson remarked in a recent cover story I wrote for Empire magazine about Dune: Part Three: “I went into it being like, ‘I want to look like an alien,’ and initially Denis was saying, ‘Well, I think he’s got to fit in with everybody. I think he just looks like you. He’s normal,’” Pattinson said. The actor was candid about his own reaction: “I was a little bit disappointed.”.

In a recent development, then Villeneuve thought about it some more. As the director told those students on Saturday, he has a strong point of view, but it’s not inflexible. Villeneuve is not interested in the whims of a crowd, but he is very open to suggestions from creative partners. If their own insights open his eyes to a possibility he hadn’t considered, he will seize upon the ideas.

According to recent reports, shortly before shooting, Villeneuve reversed course on Scytale, and Pattinson mentioned the filmmaker sent him an email with a latest look for the face-dancer. Pale skin, white hair, no eyebrows, which has the effect of making his expressions somewhat inscrutable. In other words, a blank page, upon which the characteristics of others can be written as he shifts his own natural shape. Pattinson said he felt relief: “I’m like, ‘Okay, this is very much not like a normal guy at all.’”.

Industry observers note that this anecdote is meaningful for 007 because it highlights that the filmmaker and the star can share ideas, experiment and explore, and listen to each other. That’s the collaboration this character needs.

According to recent reports, at 40, Pattinson is not the youngest possible Bond, but he brings life experience that will be vital for playing a character who needs a certain prowess and wisdom to survive. He and Villeneuve both have a kind of double-oh swagger that will allow them to ignore the cacophonous advice of the masses and devise something original.

Sources indicate that pattinson has been doing this for a long time. Consider his doomed Cedric Diggory in 2005’s Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, another character—like Bond, Bruce Wayne, and Edward Cullen—who exists as an intense, preexisting image in the minds of millions of fans. But with his brooding presence, he added uncertainty to Cedric’s innate decency and fair-mindedness. The kid who dramatically hops down from a tree in his jump-scare introduction to Ron and Harry could very well have been there to bully them. That’s a sneak attack entrance, proposed by Pattinson himself, and little details like that gave this upright, wholesome character a dose of intrigue.

It has been revealed that pattinson was only seventeen when he filmed that. In the more than two decades that followed, he has paid his dues, learned his lessons, and no doubt gotten his share of scars. With Villeneuve backing him, he’s bulletproof. The two of them can take chances, be bold, and defy orders—just like 007 would, just as playing the character demands.

Pattinson is not a paper doll that will fold when the committees come for James Bond.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, in the wake of Friday’s grounding of all flights in the continental United States and the weekend of cancellations and chaos that ensued, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy made the rounds of the Sunday morning political talk indicates to make this face.

It’s been a tough few days for Duffy, and Duffy has been huffy. From Friday’s press conference with Markwayne Mullin, to his own microphonically challenged solo outing on Saturday, through all five morning show appearances, Duffy has checked all the boxes the modern Republican official must: look aggrieved, place blame elsewhere, praise the President, be white. It’s all television, after all, and there’s a role to be played.

Sources indicate that sean Duffy has been at this for decades. You know he was on the sixth season of The Real World, and you know he met his wife and fellow Real Worlder Rachel Campos when they participated in an early season of what would become The Real World/Road Rules Challenge. But when you really go back and look, you’ll see that they’ve both been practicing for this moment since the ‘90s. Game recognizes game; as a fellow alumnus of 20th century MTV, let me walk you through it.

According to recent reports, the Real World was born when MTV decided to try its hand at creating a weekly soap opera, in the style of the era-defining Beverly Hills 90210 and Melrose Place. But cable budgets being what they are, a full scripted show was untenable, so producers had the bold idea to do away with actors and writers entirely. The first couple seasons of The Real World kept the focus on art by casting young artists: Julie the emerging dancer amid the model and writer and singer-songwriters in season one, Jon the wannabe Garth Brooks in season two. But that went out the window quick, as producers and aspiring castmates figured out the same thing at the same time: the job was to stir the pot. So by season three, deeply unpleasant bike messenger Puck was dropped into the San Francisco house to clash with saintly AIDS educator Pedro, with whom conservative Rachel initially refused to share a bathroom for fear of sink-based HIV transmission. In 1994.

By season six, casts seemed chosen specifically to play a predetermined part and drive each other up the wall: Real World: Boston features Stanford med student Kameelah and ladies’ man Syrus, Catholic Texan Elka and Manhattan-born mess on wheels Montana. And then there was Sean Duffy, Wisconsin boy, lumberjack games participant, and future Secretary of Transportation. Sean occupied the Cute Boy spot in the cast that had been held by Aaron in Los Angeles and St. Louis race car driver Mike in London. But this being 1997, he was also a different cultural archetype: the knee-jerk Rush Limbaugh-era conservative. Accent on “jerk.” Here’s a moment where Sean makes fun of Elka’s underwear and then immediately denies it.

Sources indicate that just straight-up, reflexively, smoothly denying he did something we just saw him do, because he did it on camera and into a microphone. Lying with a straight face. This would become a job skill.

It’s a little like something we saw Sean’s future wife Rachel do on her season. In an early episode, she engaged in the hot safe rebellious act of 1994 by getting her navel pierced. In a later episode, she gets a telephone call from her angry mother, who has seen the bellybutton bauble in a photograph (a physical photograph, sent through the U.S. Mail; again, we lived differently in the ‘90s). Rachel assures her mother it’s not a piercing, but instead a sticker she put there. Forget the fact that, again, all of this is on camera and the mom is going to learn the truth soon enough. Watching back then, I remember thinking two things: one, this person lies very easily, and two, I think she might be one of those people who’s conservative just so they don’t upset their parents.

Archaeologists with the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap) were excavating ahead of a residential construction project near Colmar, on the banks of the Ill River in eastern France. According to a translated statement, they found both a Gallo-Roman village occupied from the first to the third century C.E., and a fifth-century funerary complex containing 14 human burials and two horse burials.

The human burials included 11 adults or older adolescents and three children. Human bone fragments found west of the necropolis suggest that more burials may lie beyond the site’s boundaries. The burial pits were typically quadrangular or trapezoidal in shape and sized to fit the person buried inside. Some of the pits were also filled with artifacts.

Those artifacts caught the archaeologists’ attention. Two graves contained high-quality goods associated with warriors, including a sword partially preserved in a wooden scabbard, a single-edged knife, a shield, and a barbed javelin. The Inrap experts said the grave goods match those of Germanic chieftains, whose peoples allied with and joined the Roman army in the region near the Empire’s Rhine frontier during the fifth century.

The weapons and the clothing both featured decorative elements made of gold and silver and inlaid with garnets, further evidence of the high status of those buried.

Recent findings suggest that two graves associated with women also produced impressive finds, including silver-gilt bow brooches, silver bird-shaped brooches, glass-bead necklaces, belt buckles, and a bone comb. Even the horses received grave goods: harness equipment was buried with both animals.

It has been revealed that the skeletons, however, told a grimmer story, with signs of injury and poor health found throughout the 14 burials. At least two of the deceased had fractures that were never set, and one of these likely left a man’s lower leg useless. Two other individuals had bone injuries likely caused by edged weapons. “The complete absence of perilesional bone remodeling suggests that death followed these violent acts rapidly,” the experts wrote.

The team was surprised to find so many injuries linked to violence in such a small sample of burials.

Industry observers note that the fifth-century funerary complex was the excavation’s most striking discovery, but it wasn’t the only one. The team also uncovered part of the Gallo-Roman village’s core, including a residential district and a network of streets, showing that people lived there continuously from the first to the third century C.E.

It has been revealed that human activity at the site began in the middle of the first century C.E., and the site was most densely occupied from the second into the third century. Houses built of perishable materials stood on stone footings and were arranged along a street network that changed over time. Archaeologists also found hearths and wells, along with other structures that they said may have been used for industrial work.

In a recent development, after the village declined, a layer of silt covered the area. The silt shows only occasional use and little human activity through the fourth century, until the burials appeared in the fifth century.

Because evidence from this era is so rare, the funerary complex helps shed light on the poorly understood transition between the end of the Western Roman Empire and the Merovingian era in the Alsace region. “The exceptional nature of this find stems, in particular, from the scarcity of sites that document Germanic settlements during the specific chronological period in the region,” the statement reads. “These upcoming findings will undoubtedly provide a fresh impetus for examining the region’s settlement dynamics, as well as the profound upheavals that shaped this territory during the second half of the fifth century.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Dealing with menopause comes with a string of challenges and changes, but many people don’t expect acne to be one of them.
  • Suzan Obagi, a board-certified dermatologist, associate professor of dermatology and plastic surgery, and director of the UPMC Cosmetic Surgery & Skin Health Center, explains that menopausal or perimenopausal acne differs from typical acne because it localizes to the chin and upper neck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Dealing with menopause comes with a string of challenges and changes, but many people don’t expect acne to be one of them. Board-certified dermatologist Dr. Elizabeth Hale explains to ELLE that the hormonal influence that occurs during menopause can be similar to teenage acne. The difference is that the skin being treated at this stage is very different from your younger skin, and the hormonal changes are different. “As estrogen and progesterone fluctuate and decline, the relative influence of androgens like testosterone becomes more noticeable,” states Hale. “That can increase oil production and trigger breakouts even while the rest of the skin is getting drier, thinner, and more sensitive,” Hale says. She adds that teenage skin is usually oily, resilient, and tolerant of aggressive treatment.

On the other end, Dr. Suzan Obagi, a board-certified dermatologist, associate professor of dermatology and plastic surgery, and director of the UPMC Cosmetic Surgery & Skin Health Center, explains that menopausal or perimenopausal acne differs from typical acne because it localizes to the chin and upper neck. “Patients will get flares with their menses of large, tender papules and cysts that take time to resolve. By the time they do resolve, the next round comes out,” notes Obagi.

Menopausal acne also differs from the adult acne women may have had in their 20s and 30s, which often tracked with your monthly cycle. “During perimenopause, cycles become irregular, so flares can feel unpredictable,” Hale clarifies.

Industry observers note that acne at any age can be very frustrating. Obagi states this is especially true for women who have not had to contend with acne before. But left untreated, it can lead to scars, so it is imperative to try to get it under control. While it’s yet another annoyance to add to the menopause side effect checklist, menopausal acne is treatable. Hale and Obagi explain how to manage menopausal acne.

Sources indicate that according to Hale, menopausal acne usually clusters along the jawline, chin, around the mouth, and sometimes the neck. “It’s more likely to be deeper, tender, inflamed bumps that linger, rather than surface blackheads and whiteheads,” says Hale.

Sources indicate that skin renews more slowly at this stage, so blemishes can also take longer to heal. With this slow healing process, acne marks are more likely to leave behind dark marks or lingering redness. “That’s especially true for women with deeper skin tones, who are more prone to post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation,” Hale notes.

Recent findings suggest that the goal is to treat the acne without stripping the rest of the skin. Hale suggests looking for these key skin care ingredients:.

According to recent reports, obagi goes the prescription route with her patients. “Oftentimes I will discuss with my patients starting an oral anti-androgen medication called spironolactone. In high doses, it functions as a diuretic/anti-hypertensive medication,” states Obagi. However, at low doses, she explains, it seems to offset the effects of male hormones on oil glands and hair follicles. “It helps reduce the cyclical flare of hormonal acne while protecting against hair loss on the scalp,” Obaji adds.

Industry observers note that diet isn’t the main driver of menopausal acne; it’s primarily hormonal. However, Hale notes that some research has linked high-glycemic diets and dairy, particularly skim milk, to acne in some people. “A balanced diet with whole foods, adequate protein, healthy fats, and fewer refined sugars supports overall skin health,” notes Hale.

According to recent reports, increasing your protein intake for muscle and bone health at this stage of life can also prove beneficial. However, Hale warns that whey protein supplements have been associated with breakouts in some people. “If you started a protein shake around the time your breakouts began, that’s worth noticing,” Hale says.

Although it’s not a food, Obaji points out that hormonal changes from medications can also play a role in emerging breakouts, whether it’s stopping birth control or starting or changing hormone therapy. Some progestins have more androgenic activity than others, so make sure to talk to your doctor about this.

In a recent development, adjust is the key word here, not overhaul. “The good news is that many of the best antiaging ingredients are also acne-friendly,” says Hale. Retinoids, niacinamide, antioxidants, and azelaic acid all address both concerns.

Industry observers note that timing is also key. “During the monthly flares of hormonal acne, the patients may feel that their skin is temporarily more oily. They may have to adjust their topical regimen to include a cleanser designed for blemish-prone skin, such as the Veea Face Clarifying Gel Cleanser, which contains salicylic acid, witch hazel, and burdock root extract,” Obaji recommends. Also swap in a non-comedogenic moisturizer to avoid aggravating breakouts.

Hale states you also want to avoid heavy occlusives that can clog pores in breakout-prone areas, and avoid stacking too many actives, which can lead to irritation. SPF is still vital, too, so finish off your routine with a lightweight, non-comedogenic formula.

If you’re using a serum, choose a hydrating one since menopausal skin tends to be on the drier side.

Unfortunately, you can’t stop or prevent the hormonal transition, but Hale states you can reduce how often breakouts happen and how severe they are by choosing the right ingredients and adjusting your routine.

“It’s also important to support sleep and manage stress as best you can. Stress hormones can worsen breakouts, and night sweats and disrupted sleep are common and can contribute to breakouts as well,” notes Hale.

Industry observers note that although there’s no way to prevent menopausal acne, Obaji says the most notable thing is to recognize it early and treat it before it leaves any scars. “Sometimes, if a patient’s estradiol levels have dipped enough, starting on hormone replacement therapy may help offset hormonal acne,” she says.

Keep in mind, too, that most acne treatments can take 8-12 weeks to show real results, and mature skin may take a little longer to turn over, so be patient with the process and your products as you navigate menopausal acne.

#7477. AI Surveillance Could Be Harming Your Health. Here’s How.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (995 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

AI Surveillance Could Be Harming Your Health. Here’s How.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When CEOs and scientists wax poetic about the potential benefits of AI, the technology’s impact on human health often rises to the top—and in many ways, they’re not wrong.
  • However, like any tool, artificial intelligence can also be used for nefarious purposes, and a new perspective published in the New England Journal of Medicine highlights a particularly insidious one and its potential impacts on human health: mass surveillance.
  • The authors identify at least three ways surveillance harms health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When CEOs and scientists wax poetic about the potential benefits of AI, the technology’s impact on human health often rises to the top—and in many ways, they’re not wrong. Artificial intelligence’s ability to sift through massive datasets makes these algorithms ideal for spotting early-stage cancer or discovering novel drugs. The United Nations even notes that AI-powered disease surveillance could detect potential outbreaks quickly and prevent crises from spiraling into global pandemics.

However, like any tool, artificial intelligence can also be used for nefarious purposes, and a new perspective published in the New England Journal of Medicine highlights a particularly insidious one and its potential impacts on human health: mass surveillance. Debates over how governments and companies collect our personal data are usually framed as civil liberties or national security issues. But experts from Massachusetts General Hospital, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, and Harvard Medical School say that being watched can make us sick, and in the age of AI, things could get much, much worse.

The authors identify at least three ways surveillance harms health. First, knowing (or even believing) that you’re constantly being monitored can lead to hypervigilance and chronic “anticipatory stress,” which takes a toll on both physical and mental health. Second, surveillance can scare vulnerable people away from essential health behaviors. This includes groups with a reasonable fear of persecution, such as undocumented immigrants or people seeking reproductive or gender-affirming care, who may avoid pharmacies and clinics, hold back details from their doctors, or even skip buying groceries. Third, surveillance data can be used to hand out things that shape our health, like insurance, housing, and jobs, unequally.

“Historically, mass surveillance programs in the United States have most often been organized by government agencies and subject to democratic oversight,” the authors write. “AI-enabled surveillance, however, relies on data ecosystems that are controlled primarily by private companies.”.

In a recent development, that’s a major distinction. The Fourth Amendment’s protections are limited when people voluntarily share information with third parties, even if they don’t realize they’re doing so. HIPAA also generally doesn’t cover data collected by consumer-facing tech companies. As a result, AI companies and other private actors can access and analyze vast amounts of personal data, and they could share it with the government without your knowledge or permission. Traditional surveillance usually needed human oversight. AI, by contrast, can continuously comb through social media, search results, financial transactions, geolocation records, and camera footage, then combine it all into increasingly powerful predictions.

This concern isn’t without real-world precedent. The Denver-based Palantir Technologies, founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, developed AI-enabled tools for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), including a system known as ImmigrationOS. ICE has used these tools to combine information from multiple government databases, including visa histories and Medicaid records, to target people for immigration enforcement. Another tool, called Enhanced Leads Identification and Targeting for Enforcement (ELITE), pulls names, photos, addresses, and race and ethnicity data from Medicaid records to map areas with people who could be detained, according to reporting in The BMJ. It can reportedly even generate a “confidence score” for whether someone might be at home.

Industry observers note that for the authors, all this surveillance amounts to a public health problem. When data collected for health care or social services can be repurposed for surveillance, trust erodes, and people may stop using vital programs. That’s why they argue that AI-enabled mass surveillance should be considered an emerging “structural determinant of health,” which they define as a social, political, environmental, or economic condition that shapes how health and illness are distributed across a population.

“We believe medicine has an urgent responsibility to confront these developments,” the authors write. “Decisions about AI-enabled mass surveillance are being made with limited input from health experts, even though these systems have clear consequences for population health.” Health care technologies can contribute to the problem, too. Clinicians increasingly recommend wearables and smartphone apps that continuously collect patient data, which means the medical system may be feeding the same data streams that could be used for surveillance.

Still, there are ways to fight back. The authors recommend that health care institutions push policymakers for stronger health data protections. They point to Washington state’s 2023 My Health My Data Act, which extended privacy protections to some consumer health data that HIPAA doesn’t cover, including information inferred by algorithms. Nevada and Connecticut have passed similar laws. But the authors warn that these protections are limited, differ from state to state, and don’t stop government agencies from getting and using that data.

Industry observers note that the courts offer another option. More than 20 state attorneys general have sued the federal government for sharing Medicaid data with ICE and Palantir, and the authors say health care institutions can support these lawsuits by publicly opposing troubling data-sharing deals. Clinicians can also help by documenting patients’ fears about how their data is used and any resulting changes in whether they seek care, which gives litigators and policymakers evidence to work with.

According to recent reports, AI surveillance could still be a boon to public health. The same ability to rapidly pull together data from different sources that makes it dangerous could also help health officials spot and respond to threats more effectively. In the end, AI is just a tool, and it’s up to us how we use it. But the authors warn that we may not have long to decide. By the time AI surveillance’s effects become fully apparent, its infrastructure “may already be deeply embedded in everyday life.” As they put it, “The norms established today could determine whether AI-enabled surveillance becomes a tool in service to population health or a driver of avoidable health inequities and structural harm.”.

In a recent development, darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Grammys, more than any other awards-voting body of the significant EGOT four, is easily the most chaotic. Sure, we can shake our fists in the air all day about how Stanley Kubrick somehow never won an Oscar, or ask ourselves why the Tony Awards ever allowed itself to become a place where SpongeBob Squarepants: The Broadway Musical leads with twelve nominees. But recalling Grammy events like Macklemore beating Kendrick Lamar, Esperanza Spalding claiming Best Latest Artist over Justin Bieber and Drake, and Beck taking home Album of the Year instead of Beyoncé, it’s a wonder just what happens between when the votes are submitted and when the winners are revealed.

This year? The Recording Academy announced on Monday, November 16, that Kanye West is a Grammy nominee once again. And there’s a single category where Bruce Springsteen, Phoebe Bridgers, and Charli XCX are lumped together, so I guess they’re considered basically the same kind of artist to voters. Plus, newly introduced ideas like “Best Asian Pop Music Performance” are moving forward despite immediately losing support from the most prominent artist in that category, and Best New Artist nominees can apparently put out their fifth studio album and still be considered. What’s going on?

So, before the Grammys decide to ignore all of our desires and complaints and just shower Taylor Swift with more little golden phonographs on February 7, 2027, let’s try to make sense of the 2026 Grammy nominees below.

The first thought that entered my mind when I saw this year’s nominees for Album of the Year was, Are we confirming who will be available to perform before announcing the nominees now? Because even if so, I think Bruno Mars would perform either way.

Industry observers note that it’s very cool to see how women dominated the music field this year, especially because they truly did. Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers, and Rosalía all earning Album of the Year nominations is a no-brainer. Olivia Dean, who won Best Upcoming Artist last year, and Ella Langley, who wrote “Choosin’ Texas,” make up the rest of the list. (Did we really love that entire nineteen-track Langley album?) Plus, of course, the obligatory Taylor Swift nominations.

But were Bruno Mars and Leon Thomas—who are tied with seven nominations each after the leading women, including an Album of the Year nod for Mars—the two men with the best offerings this year?

In a recent development, bruno Mars had a very good song on The Romantic with “Why You Wanna Fight?” The Luther Vandross-esque R&B ballad was everything you’d look for in a Song of the Year nominee. But instead, it looks like Bruno is going all in on “Risk It All” and “I Just Might,” the latter of which is more of a “Happy” by Pharrell Williams-type song that somehow isn’t the lead single of the next Trolls movie.

Sorry Madonna! Apologies Robyn, Tinashe, Slayyter, and every other pop artist who soundtracked our year on the dance floor with some of the best albums of 2026. Breaking into the top four major categories still looks like a no-go.

Recent findings suggest that instead, Madonna, Robyn, and Tinashe were relegated to categories such as Best Dance Pop Recording and Best Dance/Electronic Album, even despite critical acclaim. If you want a Record of the Year nod, try writing a song for Toy Story 5.

Don Toliver is up for Best Upcoming Artist. The Houston rapper, who was signed to Travis Scott’s label in 2018, released his fifth studio album, Octane, this year. He had a song on the F9 soundtrack in 2021—which isn’t even the latest Fast & Furious movie—and his 2023 album, Love Sick, featured James Blake, Future, and Justin Bieber. But here we are, in 2026, watching him compete for Best New Artist.

In a recent development, equally puzzling: Remi Wolf is nominated for Best Fresh Artist. The singer’s exceptional debut record, Juno, came out in 2021. And her best record to date, Mud, was released recently on October 9, just outside of the Grammy submission window that closed in late August. But following the logic of how Olivia Dean won Best New Artist last year even though Dean’s album is competing this year, it’s clear that the whole Best New Artist category needs some rethinking.

Recent findings suggest that 2026 wasn’t a banner year for rap. I can admit that. Sure, we had very good records from A$AP Rocky, Denzel Curry, Vince Staples, JPEGMAFIA, Isaiah Rashad, Genesis Owusu, and Baby Keem. But none of the musicians I listed above went recognized this year, except for Keem’s single “Best Rap Performance” nomination.

According to recent reports, instead, the Recording Academy nominated Wale’s Everything Is a Lot—the Washington, D.C., rapper’s best and most mature album of the last decade, but far less influential than Rocky’s or Keem’s releases. And if not for Drake’s long-running boycott, the absence of Iceman’s “Janice STFU” just looks silly. But if you want to talk ridiculous, let’s see how Rap Album of the Year nominee Kanye West plays out for the Recording Academy over the next couple of months.

Industry observers note that harry Styles won Album of the Year for Harry’s House in 2023. He beat out Un Verano Sin Ti by Bad Bunny, Renaissance by Beyoncé, Mr. Morale & the Massive Steppers by Kendrick Lamar, and 30 by Adele. It was a major upset. And just last month, the former One Direction member wrapped a historic thirty-night residency at Madison Square Garden in New York City in support of his latest album, Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.

Now, I’m not saying Kiss All the Time is a masterwork, but it’s strange that Styles didn’t receive a single nomination for his Harry’s House follow-up. “Aperture” was very catchy! Taylor Swift can’t sneeze without the Recording Academy inventing a fresh category for her to compete in. But an artist who just won Album of the Year can find himself completely shut out, even if his latest record is a success?

The global K-pop megastars reunited this year following mandatory military service in South Korea for one of the genre’s most-anticipated albums of all time, ARIRANG. The record paid homage to the popular Korean folk song of the same name while also pushing the K-pop genre forward with hip-hop-heavy material. ARIRANG’s fourteen tracks also filled the top fourteen spots of Spotify's global Top 50 chart on its first day of release on March 20. I’ll stop there, but there are a hundred more ways to say that it was one of the biggest albums of the year.

In a recent development, but when the Recording Academy announced a upcoming category this year, “Best Asian Pop Music Performance,” the group made the decision not to submit for the Grammys this year. The move was widely regarded as a protest of the new category, which many interpreted as a ghettoization to combat the rise of popular Asian acts away from the general field categories. “I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language,” the group posted on social media.

Industry observers note that on Monday, November 16, the Academy went through with the category anyway, announcing nominees including LISA from Blackpink, the Japanese pop-metal group Babymetal, the K-pop group IVE, and the Filipino girl group Bini, among others. But with BTS joining Drake in his boycott of the Grammys, I wonder how the Recording Academy will fare without two of the world’s most popular acts entertaining their awards show.

Sources indicate that the Great Divide, a seventeen-track rock album that turned Kahan into one of the most popular touring musicians of 2026, was considered a favorite to receive a nomination in every major category this year. Songs like “American Cars” dealt with past failures and roadtrip blues, while lead single “The Great Divide” tackled how fame added extra struggles to many of his already-strained relationships. And Kahan had the resume to become a major category contender this year. He had a Number One record! He did the full press tour, he performed on Saturday Night Live, and he sold out stadiums all across the country.

But it must have been an omen when Kahan sang that “California’s so much more than some awards show” on the deluxe edition’s “Orbiter,” because he received just one nomination on Monday for Best Contemporary Folk Album. It’s a shame.

Best Album Cover is back. The category returned last year and accurately awarded Tyler, the Creator’s zany Chromakopia artwork, which featured the artist wearing a black, ceramic mask. He told Complex at the time that it symbolized how the latest music was “so honest, that I think I had to wear a mask of my own face to get some of that sh*t out.”.

It has been revealed that but what about this year’s nominees? Well, Mavis Staples’s Sad and Beautiful World artwork depicts the artist sitting at a table. Interpol’s This Mirror Weighs a Ton artwork is a chandelier made of security cameras, and Lily Allen’s West End Girl is a painting of the artist wearing a polkadot jacket. Are these nominees... the best album covers of the year?

Industry observers note that charli XCX’s photograph of Martin Scorsese, John Cale, and Marc Jacobs was easily the much-talked about album cover of the year, even though Music, Fashion, Film wasn’t nominated. Olivia Rodrigo’s upside-down swinging for you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love is definitely one of the more memorable covers that come to mind. Same goes for Robyn’s blurry and nude Sexistential photo, the politics behind Kneecap’s Fenian, Thundercat biting his dark leather jacket on the cover of Distracted, or even a pregnant Latto posing with a baby tiger for the Substantial Mama cover ahead of her cheetah-themed baby shower.

According to recent reports, we might not have a specific shade of green to color this year and make Best Album Cover an easy choice, but if you’re going to bring the category back? At least wow us.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man received double the surprise when they uncovered a 1,100-year-old double grave.
  • “This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” Allison Fox noted in a statement.
  • Recent findings suggest that experts believe the metal detectorists, Daniel Crowe and Rhett Britton, came upon the double grave of a man and a woman who were buried with some of their finest possessions: three brooches for her and a sword for him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man received double the surprise when they uncovered a 1,100-year-old double grave. It contained rare brooches typically worn by Scandinavian women and a sword that, according to one expert, would once have gleamed with a “bright silver” pommel. The site also produced intricately decorated trading weights, a Viking axe head, balance scales, and a ceremonial bronze ladle.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” Allison Fox noted in a statement. Fox is curator for archaeology at Manx National Heritage, a museum and heritage trust on the Isle of Man, a self-governing British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland. “What makes it particularly exciting is the combination of finds, which gives us a rare opportunity to explore the lives of some of the island’s earliest Scandinavian settlers.”.

Recent findings suggest that experts believe the metal detectorists, Daniel Crowe and Rhett Britton, came upon the double grave of a man and a woman who were buried with some of their finest possessions: three brooches for her and a sword for him. Fox stated the date of the brooches suggests the grave may be the “earliest known female Viking Age burial” on the island. Together with the other finds, she said, the objects “help us build a picture of the people who lived here more than a thousand years ago, how they traded, and the connections they maintained across the Viking world.”.

The find dates to around 900 C.E. That places it at the early end of the Viking Age on the Isle of Man, just as Scandinavian communities were becoming established there. Some of the objects are also the first of their kind found on the island.

In a recent development, museum experts believe the Vikings first arrived on the island during the ninth century. Recognizing the strategic importance of its location in the Irish Sea, they established trading links before settling there. A rich Viking heritage remains across the island, and burials found in the past show evidence of pagan traditions. Viking influence still runs through Manx culture today. Tynwald, the island’s parliament, was founded during the Viking Age and is known as one of the world’s oldest continuous parliaments.

After making their discovery, Crowe and Britton didn’t try to clean the objects. Fox claims this has allowed experts to fully appreciate the objects’ intricate details. She added that the brooches still have soil inside them, and the team is carefully excavating it in hopes of finding traces of textile.

In a recent development, two of the brooches are a matching pair of oval “tortoise” brooches, the kind Scandinavian women wore to fasten their dresses at the shoulders. Both are covered in intricate interlocking animals, a hallmark of Viking art. According to Manx National Heritage, only one other pair like them has ever been found on the Isle of Man, and that was found by Daniel Crowe’s own father, John Crowe, along with fellow metal detectorist Craig Evans. The latest pair is likely about 50 years older, which is why experts think this grave may be the island’s earliest known female Viking burial. The third brooch, decorated with spirals and a glass center, is the first of its kind found on the island.

In a recent development, the sword is the type a man would have carried, and it’s the 13th Viking sword found on the Isle of Man. Although the blade is badly corroded and parts of it are missing entirely, Fox noted in a video from the heritage group that the pommel still reveals “signs of the really intricate decorating that would have been on the pommel when it was buried.” X-ray analysis revealed traces of silver and copper wire inlaid into the iron, which makes it one of only three swords found on the island with such decoration.

“When this sword was buried,” she said, “this top part of the sword would have been really bright silver, a really high-status object.” In addition, traces of wood show that the sword’s handle was covered in wood rather than thread or horn.

Although 1,100 years in the ground caused much of the sword’s damage, experts believe the Vikings broke it on purpose as part of a burial ritual.

Sources indicate that because the brooches were found alongside the sword (items linked to a woman and a man, respectively), a double burial seems likely. Experts said, however, that they can’t be sure whether the grave goods came from one grave or from two graves placed close together.

Sources indicate that beyond the burial itself, the decorated lead weights and bronze balance scales found at the site highlight the Isle of Man’s role in Irish Sea trade. The weights are the first of their kind found on the island. One of them has a decorative bronze fitting, with artwork typical of Britain and Ireland, that may have been taken from another object.

The bronze ladle, another first for the island, was likely used in ceremonies.

Despite all the experts have gleaned from the discovery, there’s still much to be learned. “Although the original burial site has been disturbed,” Fox remarked, “further research may reveal much more about these objects and the people who owned them.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association indicates it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart complications, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

According to recent reports, of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

Industry observers note that they also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

Makita 12-Inch Snow Shovel Attachment.

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Recent findings suggest that most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

Sources indicate that with a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it releases snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

In a recent development, on the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

In a recent development, though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

Industry observers note that it packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

Sources indicate that if you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

Recent findings suggest that at 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

It has been revealed that ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was rapidly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

Sources indicate that we must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

It has been revealed that along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

In a recent development, with its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For significant jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

It has been revealed that when push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That remarked, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

In a recent development, much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Recent findings suggest that electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you strategy to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

In a recent development, electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

In a recent development, similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side.

Sources indicate that the average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It has been revealed that it’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.
