📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In a recent development, for years, Ronny Kobo has turned to Brooks Brothers for one piece in particular: a white tuxedo jacket. “If you know a good white tuxedo menswear jacket, the best in the market is available at Brooks Brothers,” the designer tells ELLE. “Every couple of years I refreshed my wardrobe with a white tuxedo men’s size 50. And when I went to the store about a year ago, I started to daydream and I was thinking, wouldn’t it be amazing to collaborate with Brooks Brothers?”.

Industry observers note that that daydream wasn’t far-fetched; it became the starting point for Kobo’s holiday 2026 capsule with Brooks Brothers. Reworking the brand’s tuxedo and evening wear codes through a feminine lens, the collection gives sharp tailoring, satin lapels, and classic tartan a softer turn in fluid dresses and statement-making separates.

For Kobo, the collaboration was an opportunity to pair Brooks Brothers’ menswear heritage with tried-and-true holiday codes, from green and red tartan to silk bow details, clichés and all.

“Holiday dressing should be about the cliches,” she notes. “What’s fun is showing up to a holiday party in a cliche. That’s what makes your holiday your holiday party. Let’s create something that is so holiday in your closet that you take out every holiday for the rest of your fashion life.”.

In a recent development, despite those seasonal touches, many of the pieces can be worn year-round. Tailored staples, including a series of tuxedo jackets and formal trousers, work well beyond the holidays. Accessories feel just as seasonless, with cummerbunds, leather opera gloves, and a red rosette brooch bringing a touch of occasion to a look in any season.

According to recent reports, the designer achieved that year-round appeal through pieces that can be styled more than one way. Kobo’s take on the white tuxedo jacket is elongated and nipped at the waist, doubling as a minidress; it could just as easily be layered with the high-waisted Ruby pant or worn over the sheer lace Beryl top. The collection is made for “going out,” with dressier options including a high-low skirt with a cummerbund waist, a fitted LBD with a red sash, and the Lazuli dress, a body-conscious stretch-satin number with a flouncy peplum.

The collection’s mix-and-match pieces reflect Kobo’s belief that black tie should leave room for individual expression.

“Allowing your personal style to shine through these tuxedo moments is really crucial,” she says. “Men get to show up in black tie and express their personality in such a quiet, elegant way, because you can’t put too much on a tuxedo jacket. With this collection, we’re just supplying the canvas. I’d love to see how everyone styles it, whether with lace stockings, velvet, or some kind of conversation piece that feels authentic to you.”.

The best men's parka is a lot like an upright sleeping bag, except it doesn't simply keep you insulated. It also protects your frostbite-prone fits from Mother Nature’s icy clutches, and keeps you looking sharp in the process. Don't believe us? Just ask the parka's most loyal servant: Oasis frontman Liam Gallagher.

Before giving you our favourites, some quick history: Parkas originated in the Arctic, where the Inuit designed them to withstand bone-chilling temperatures. They then made their way to the US military with the introduction of the N-3B parka in the 1950s. Throughout its evolution, the parka's mission has remained unchanged: to keep not just your torso warm, but your thighs and rear end too. Seriously, you've already worn that waist-length puffer to death: Make like Justin Jefferson. Go long.

Recent findings suggest that the North Face McMurdo down parka isn’t just another winter coat—it’s a cold-weather icon with Antarctic-level credibility. Named after McMurdo Station, the US research hub in Antarctica, this parka is designed to thrive in below-freezing temperatures while keeping you comfortable and protected. With 600-fill recycled down insulation and windproof, waterproof, and breathable DryVent technology, it’s eco-friendly armor for the tundra—or the Target parking lot. Made from recycled nylon and polyester, it’s part of The North Face’s recycled-repurpose collection, combining sustainability with serious performance.

Sources indicate that loaded with features like six exterior pockets, a removable faux-fur ruff, an adjustable hood, and a draft flap, this 3.5-pound powerhouse is your portable fortress of warmth. Stylish touches like the midnight petrol color elevate it above standard winter fare, while practical details make it indispensable for everything from scraping windshields to tackling arctic adventures. Whether you’re braving brutal weather or commuting in comfort, the McMurdo is built to last—complete with The North Face’s warranty to keep it in the game longer than your ever-disappearing gloves.

Mountain Hardwear has been a staple in the outdoor gear world long before its sold-out collaboration with Stüssy (though they’ve probably gained a few new fans in the process). Founded in 1993 in Richmond, California, the brand spun off from the well-known outdoor firm Sierra Designs. A group of designers and engineers left Sierra Designs to create Mountain Hardwear, and 32 years later, it’s still famous for its technical outerwear, sleeping bags, and pioneering use of Gore-Tex.

This jacket is built for camping, featuring a durable ripstop shell and 650-fill down. With a fully adjustable insulated hood and a drawcord at the waist to trap in heat, it’s tough to top even before you encounter the two BYO-bevvy pockets—specially designed to carry your favorite beverages. Whether you're in your tent or Air Streamer, this jacket keeps you warm—and your drinks cold—so you can stay cozy and hydrated in style.

Woolrich: So good it doesn't need a logo patch. The American outdoor firm was founded in 1830, and since then has become the destination for warmth-minded men who don't need anyone else to know they're walking around in the very best materials.

Which isn't to say this parka won't turn some heads. New for this season, it comes in seven colors, from a stunning light blue to nutty falcon brown, and also boasts some envy-inducing hand-warmer pockets, hidden rib-knit cuffs, and even a water-repellent finish. (A nice touch for a style that typically is more preoccupied with keeping out the cold than the wet.) One more thing: It's called the Cloud because it's incredibly light, even with a 90/10 duck down fill. A winter coat that wears like a summer-weight hoodie? Worth the investment.

This is the kind of Canada Goose jacket that reminds you why the brand is so much more than just a status symbol for finance guys. (Though I'm sure they don't mind being that too.) For one, it's done away with that ubiquitous blue and red logo, and replaced it with a more understated, tonal patch. But that's actually the only thing that's been stripped back here: Otherwise, this parka is packed full of features, from ribbed knit cuffs, to pockets everywhere you look, to a bevy of insulation considerations, from the 625 Fill Down interior all the way to the soft, lined chin guard—a nice touch.

Available this season in Black, Olive, and Desert Sand (above), it's backed by Canada Goose's lifetime guarantee. So, yes, you're spending a fortune. But the brand stands ready to make sure you'll never need to buy another parka again.

Sources indicate that the Japanese label FrizmWORKS has reimagined a classic, ‘60s‐era expedition parka silhouette—quilted down, hard-wearing cotton-blend shell, boxy hooded cut—and, sixty years later, given it a whole fresh life. From the tonal matte finish to the utilitarian drawcord hem, this is a mountain‐camp relic reimagined for your 2025 commute. It’s rugged without resorting to SSX Tricky branding, and along with the requisite down filling also has two fun, unexpected and large pockets on the back. It also comes in a joyful orange color, if that black is a little too subtle for you.

I can't be the only one who was excited to see Reigning Champ get back into making real clothes. (Though, let’s be honest, the brand’s sweatsuits are still some of my favorites.) But this high-powered, goose-filled nylon parka? It's built for Canadian winters, which means it’ll easily thrive anywhere else, too. Technically, that means 700 fill power down, and a weather-repellent nylon shell to keep out wind and rain, as well as the colder temps. Its defining feature is its stealthy, all-black appearance, and Reigning Champ has leant hard into that vibe, with hidden interior pockets, concealed rib cuffs, and a shock cord hood that you can pull as tight as you like. Now you see me, now you don't.

Recent findings suggest that the new kids on the parka block, Major Rock Candy Mountaineering, are bringing the fun back with their vibrant, winter parka colors. These extreme cold-weather parkas take inspiration from mid-century American outdoor brands. Can’t think of any off the top of your head? Skim through a book like this, and you’ll catch the vibe.

BRCM’s parkas are packed with cozy duck down and feature a 100% grosgrain shell. This ribbed texture, courtesy of its tight weave, makes the fabric tough as nails and resistant to wear and tear. The ginormous pockets? Perfect for stashing your winter accessories (or your snacks). And if the wind has you feeling like it’s got something to prove, just tighten up the drawstring waist, hood, and hem. One of the coolest features? The jacket’s silhouette. When cinched, you can clasp your bag around the waist—ideal for those who love a good backpacking adventure. Although BRCM is still a fresh face in the outerwear world, it already feels like an instant classic.

Industry observers note that getting your hands on one of the first-ever parkas is basically impossible—right up there with finding your keys when you’re already late. Enter The Real McCoy’s, which somehow pulls it off with museum-grade reproductions. Every detail is obsessively dialed, down to the DuPont-developed nylon shell that helped kick off the whole modern-materials era.

Today’s outdoor companies are still trying to capture Patagonia’s lightning-in-a-bottle formula from when the brand first burst onto the scene: Be nice to everyone, make products the right way, and design jackets built to last forever. Take its Glacier parka, for example: it’s weatherproof, cozy enough to double as a sleeping bag, and so comfortable you might consider skipping the tent altogether.

If you’re after a quieter, minimalist parka—and you’ve got the budget—the Therme Parka delivers. It’s hip-length, packed with goose down, and built with the brand’s more environmentally friendly GORE-TEX ePE fabric, meaning it’s primed to handle a lifetime of winters.

It has been revealed that the Alpha Industries N-3B is the real-deal snorkel parka—because it is the real deal. Produced early in the company's history in the 1950s, the parka is still tough as nails and loaded with reinforced elbow patches, a full-length storm flap, and snug inset knit cuffs that keep wind firmly in its place.

Founded in 1960, Fjällräven are sort of Sweden's Patagonia. By which we mean they've always thought about three things: High-performance materials, a reasonable enough price point, and dressing it all up in some great primary colors.

Nanga is your favorite outerwear brand’s favorite outerwear brand. Its parka riffs on the US Air Force’s N-3B flight jacket, upgraded with AuroraTex—a high-performance fabric that keeps you dry no matter what. Add handwarmer pockets and a discreet cigar pouch, and you’ve got a parka that nails the perfect blend between utility and style.

Sources indicate that goldwin is so good, it literally owns the North Face in Japan. (Like, literally.) This handsome down parka is wind-blocking, body-warming, and equipped with a PERTEX Quantum ripstop lining (and shell) to prevent the tears and rips that lightweight fabrics can otherwise be prone to.

Sources indicate that berghaus' Meru jacket—which is long enough to qualify as a parka in our book—is packed with retro styling, from the color blocks to the cinchable waistband. 2L Gore-Tex means you could wear it up any peak, but its general aura means you could also wear it up on stage, hands behind your back, tambourine on your head.

In a recent development, montbell's mastery of lightweight, easy-to-rock, nicely-priced outdoors gear has become its calling card, and it’s on full display here. This down parka is easy to incorporate into pretty much any wardrobe, and even has some nice-looking stitching (which, by the way, the heads call ‘baffling’).

Industry observers note that what do you get when you cross a parka with a fireman jacket? A full-scale compliment magnet.

Industry observers note that first and foremost: functionality. A great parka should incorporate more features than a midnight infomercial. In the outer shell, you’ll typically find materials like nylon or polyester, and sometimes more rugged options like Gore-Tex. But it's also worth peeking under the hood—literally. Parkas are usually filled with down (duck or goose feathers) or synthetic insulation like polyester. Down is warm and lightweight, but it’s the fair-weather friend of insulation—it falters when wet. Synthetic insulations, on the other hand, is the ride-or-die option, keeping you warm even when soggy.

Hoods are another essential feature. Most will be made of a weatherproof fabric, and some come equipped with fluffy genuine- or faux-fur trims that gently tickle your face with a touch of winter luxury. And then there are the pockets—no one wants to walk around in a blizzard with frozen fingers. (Look for fleece linings.) Finally, asses the length. Longer parkas offer more warmth and protection from the elements, while shorter ones are perfect for commuters who need to dodge frostbite without overheating on the subway.

In a recent development, while function is the defining characteristic of a good parka, a great one should also give your winter fits a serious upgrade. Pair it with a thermal and a chunky sweater for a no-brainer look, or go bold by layering it over a denim jacket, adding corduroys, and anchoring with sturdy boots.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

It has been revealed that our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

It has been revealed that to kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

According to recent reports, we lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Sources indicate that whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.).

A NASA Veteran Claims to Have Used Mind-Bending Physics to Conquer Gravity

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in April 2024, Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist who helped establish a laboratory at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, made a remarkable claim.
  • As we reported in our earlier coverage, Buhler’s claim would have big consequences for spaceflight.
  • According to recent reports, one physicist has spent years investigating similar claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in April 2024, Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist who helped establish a laboratory at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, made a remarkable claim. His company, Exodus Propulsion Technologies, had built a device that could produce thrust without expelling propellant. He attributed the push to what he called a “Upcoming Force.”.

As we reported in our earlier coverage, Buhler’s claim would have big consequences for spaceflight. That promise depends on whether researchers outside Exodus can reproduce the push and rule out an ordinary explanation.

According to recent reports, one physicist has spent years investigating similar claims. Martin Tajmar, a professor and chair of space systems at Dresden University of Technology in Germany, has spent two decades measuring the forces produced by charged capacitors, including lopsided ones like the designs Buhler describes.

“It’s all negative,” he tells Popular Mechanics. Meaning, his tests found no evidence of that force within the limits of his equipment. He hasn’t tested Exodus’s hardware, but his experiments show what an independent test would need to account for.

In a recent development, A capacitor stores electric charge. Apply a high enough voltage to certain designs, and they can set the surrounding air moving, producing a push on the device itself. Tajmar calls this corona wind, “a discharge in air that drags air molecules with it.” In those cases, the device moves by pushing air backward, much as a fan does.

Tajmar’s team wanted to see whether a capacitor would still produce a push with almost all the air removed. For their 2024 study in Scientific Reports, they put the capacitor and its battery-powered electrical equipment together on a sensitive balance inside a vacuum chamber. At 10,000 volts, an asymmetric capacitor produced no clear sign of an unexplained force, even with instruments sensitive enough to detect a push measured in billionths of a newton.

Recent findings suggest that exodus hasn’t sent Tajmar a device, so he built his own capacitors for those experiments. He says his asymmetric design follows the principles in the organization’s patent, though he doesn’t know the exact dimensions of its hardware.

“It’s Exodus who have to say why my asymmetric capacitor does not produce any thrust,” he says.

He believes his results challenge the firm’s explanation, but he’d need its hardware to put its particular device through the same checks.

The whole experiment has to behave.

Industry observers note that keeping the battery and high-voltage equipment on the balance removes outside power cables that could interfere with the reading. Researchers also have to watch for electromagnetic forces or parts shifting as they heat up, either of which could look like thrust.

It has been revealed that tajmar also recommends swapping the device for an electrical dummy that draws power but should produce no thrust. If the balance still registers a push, something else in the setup is causing it. Researchers would need to track that down before treating the reading as evidence of a working drive.

Buhler has also said the devices can keep producing thrust after the power is switched off. Electrical charge can linger in insulating materials, leaving an electric field even after the supply is disconnected. Researchers would need to work out whether that leftover charge explains the reading and, if there really is a push, where it comes from.

In a short white paper, Exodus claims other experimenters have reproduced the effect and argues that the device pushes against the vacuum itself, allowing momentum to be conserved. But it doesn’t include their laboratory reports. Without those details, readers can’t tell how the experiments were done or whether the researchers ruled out other causes of the push.

What leaving the propellant behind could change.

Spacecraft have to bring along the propellant they’ll use to speed up, slow down or change course. That adds weight, which takes more propellant to move. The rocket equation puts numbers to that trade-off, showing how much a spacecraft can change its speed with the supply it carries.

In a recent development, if a drive could produce useful thrust without using up propellant, engineers could plan missions differently. A spacecraft could keep changing course as long as it had enough power and the drive kept working. Some of the weight now devoted to propellant tanks and their contents could go toward other equipment.

It has been revealed that but the drive would bring its own baggage. It would need a power source and a way to get rid of waste heat, and all of that would have to travel with it. Engineers would need to find out whether the thrust was worth the weight of the complete system. Getting a reliable push in the lab would give them a reason to start working that out.

Light can give a spacecraft a push, too. When a laser sends light in one direction, the laser gets a tiny push in the other, because light carries momentum. Tajmar points out that this already offers a way to produce thrust without using up material propellant.

“If you just power a laser with the power that we use in our experiments, the thrust is also propellantless and actually already exists,” he says.

The catch is how much power it takes. To hold up a 1.2-ounce object, roughly the weight of the devices Buhler described, a laser would need to send about 100 million watts of light downward. A drive that produced a useful push with much less power would be worth engineers’ attention. Researchers would also have to explain what carries momentum in the opposite direction, as the light does for a laser.

According to recent reports, “You have to test it in an independent laboratory. And then with a different method,” Tajmar says. He wants the results published so other experts can examine the work, including the equipment itself. Getting the same push on a different instrument would help show that the device deserves the credit.

Sources indicate that nobody needs to make the whole apparatus float. Even a small sideways push would warrant attention if it survived those checks and other researchers could reliably reproduce it. Then engineers could start asking whether it was strong enough to put to work aboard a spacecraft.

According to recent reports, buhler’s claim promises freedom from the propellant tank, which would change how we travel through space. The next move is closer to home. Put the drive in another lab, let someone else take the controls, and see whether the promise still has any push behind it.

The Men on 'The Gilded Age' Don't Deserve Your Praise

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it feels like television reveals (and real life, let’s face it) are currently overrun with men who constantly fall short when it comes to matters of the heart.
  • Recent findings suggest that we may only be a few episodes into the season, yet already viewers have witnessed several examples where the men in the show are found lacking when it comes to their romantic partnerships.
  • Many fans online have been quick to come to Larry’s defense, criticizing Marian for self-sabotaging or playing the part of a martyr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it feels like television reveals (and real life, let’s face it) are currently overrun with men who constantly fall short when it comes to matters of the heart. In the latest season of Nobody Wants This, many fans noticed how Joanne was constantly making sacrifices for their relationship while Noah just… wasn’t. The latest season of Love Is Blind also found the guys seriously wanting, with many failing to put in a bare minimum of effort to make a love connection. And it saddens me to say that this trend of low-effort men seems to have made its way to the fourth season of The Gilded Age as well. That’s right, my friends—not even the 19th century is safe from this epidemic of male apathy.

Recent findings suggest that we may only be a few episodes into the season, yet already viewers have witnessed several examples where the men in the show are found lacking when it comes to their romantic partnerships. First, there’s Larry, who appears to have zero appreciation for the tough position Marian is now in after they spent the night together. Although he does suggest they get married, Marian worries it’s only out of obligation, and he seems to not really grasp the severity of the situation she’s in, that social ruin could be waiting for her if anyone found out about their night together.

Many fans online have been quick to come to Larry’s defense, criticizing Marian for self-sabotaging or playing the part of a martyr. But I disagree. Her concerns are valid and Larry is being ambiguous about his feelings. Now would be the perfect time for a grand romantic gesture on Larry’s part to show Marian how serious he is about their relationship. Where’s the massive, swoonworthy “You have bewitched me body and soul” moment? Where is the standing-outside-her-window-with-a-boombox (or 1800s equivalent) scene? I want to root for them, but Larry is making it extremely difficult with his underwhelming devotion.

Then there’s Hector, who was praised by Bertha for choosing to save Gladys’s life over their unborn child’s during an extremely difficult labor. While it is nice to know how much affection he has for his wife, it never should’ve been his choice to begin with, so applauding him for “saving” Gladys feels like a very low bar to set for these male characters. I understand this was a customary practice at the time and him making the decision was more the doctor’s doing than anything else, but now he’s also gatekeeping that she can’t have any more children. Watching a man determine when a woman should know something about her own body feels outrageous in any time period. I’m not saying that Hector is a bad guy, but I don’t think he deserves so much admiration for doing the bare minimum.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, George Russell continues to deal with (or rather, not deal with) his ongoing laudanum addiction, which is already growing tiresome with each passing episode. His relationship with Bertha has never been worse. She is putting in all the effort to repair their marriage while he remains cold and distant, lying to her at every turn. I understand this change in his behavior is due to his drug dependency, but should that make all of his missteps completely forgivable? Bertha assured him at the end of Sunday night’s episode, “I won’t disappoint you.” But it is he who is the disappointment right now.

In a recent development, unfortunately, not even Dr. William Kirkland can get a free pass, despite his impeccable behavior leading up to his wedding day. Buying Peggy a house, standing up to his mother, and refusing to let her dictate the wedding — those are all major green flags. Yet next week’s promo indicated William might pursue a latest job in Washington, which feels completely out of nowhere considering he just bought a house for the two of them. Also, this is something he should probably consult his wife about before making any public declarations. Is the honeymoon phase over already?

Bottom line: Chivalry may not be completely dead on this show, but its pulse is weak at best and if these gentlemen don’t do something about it soon we’re going to have even bigger problems than prematurely pouring milk into someone else’s tea.

On Sunday night, Hollywood gathered at the Ray Dolby Ballroom in Los Angeles to celebrate artists whose work has shaped film, and the stars dressed aptly for the occasion.

This year, the Academy honored actor Glenn Close, animator Floyd Norman, and director Ridley Scott with Honorary Awards. Producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler received the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. But before the awards were presented, stars galore arrived on the red carpet in their finest finery.

Zendaya kick-started her Dune: Part Three press tour in a gilded amber gown from the archive of the British designer Giles Deacon. The actress paired the sculptural, hip-forward look with dazzling Chopard jewelry and a slim Rolex timepiece. Elsewhere, ELLE Women in Hollywood honorees Penélope Cruz, Julianne Moore, Florence Pugh, Carrie Coon, and Inde Navarette brought the fashion in Chanel, Bottega Veneta, Valentino, Balenciaga, and Dior, respectively. Primary hues—particularly a stark cherry red color—proved to be a popular choice among stars, most notably Charlize Theron, in Givenchy by Sarah Burton, and Lea Seydoux, who dazzled in a Louis Vuitton train gown. The evening also made room for menswear, with style gurus Pedro Pascal and Alexander Skarsgård rewriting the rules of black-tie dressing in unconventional looks by Chanel and Tom Ford.

Here, the 13 best-dressed stars at the 2026 Governors Awards.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that belmont Cameli wasn’t playing around when he arrived at GQ’s Breakouts Party in a beige, flecked Jacquemus and a low-cut black tank. He kept the accessories minimal: a gold pinky signet ring, his signature curls, and a short, thick mustache. Since his buzzy role in the Amazon television series Off Campus, Cameli has spent the show’s promo tour experimenting with a variety of facial hair styles. He’s gone full beard, five o’clock shadow, and, as of late, donned a mustache. He first showed off his fuzzy upper lip in mid-October at the 6th Annual Academy Museum Gala, where it was barely a whisper. By last night, it was fully formed, a couple weeks shy of hitting Tom Selleck-levels of bushy.

Sources indicate that the actor gathered with a who’s who of young breakout talents named in GQ’s annual Man of the Year glitch at the Sheats-Goldstein residence Wednesday night in Los Angeles to celebrate their spotlight-stealing achievements in entertainment, music, podcasting, and more. Cameli, for example, had a major moment as a lovable (and yes, hot) hockey player in Amazon’s hit television show Off Campus.

The fashion crowd has been embracing a hairy upper lip of late, and for good reason: When styled appropriately and kept tidy, mustaches go a long way to channel charm, confidence, and sex appeal. They also lend wearers a touch of maturity.

That might explain why there was no shortage of mustaches at last night’s bash. Fellow Breakouts member Stavros Halkias kept his signature handlebar look for the event, paired with some light stubble, while musician 54 Ultra matched his full-bodied mustache with an equally on-trend shag mullet and a healthy dosage of chest hair peeking from his unbuttoned dress shirt.

Sources indicate that the prominence of scruff, stubble, and ’staches was a clear sign that facial hair isn’t going anywhere soon. If anything, it’s the breakout grooming look of the year.
